The Flame Design study considers an innovative method of approaching combustion to address 
these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding 
of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best 
optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. 
 
Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame, in that the relationship between 
the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish the desired objective. This

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 
44 
 
 
method involves shifting the nitrogen from the air (or oxygen/nitrogen mixture) to the fuel 
stream, such that the mixing that occurs at the flame can be varied with or without affecting the 
flame temperature. [This can also be done with inerts other than nitrogen and oxygen/inert 
mixtures other than air.] Such nitrogen exchange has enabled the production of the flames that 
are soot-free at all flow conditions, i.e., which are ‘permanently blue.’ 
 
The Flame Design experiment involves gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on a 
porous spherical burner. Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits are obtained as 
functions of the nitrogen exchange, flow direction, and pressure. Extensive analytical and 
computational modeling support the experimental investigation, where they are facilitated by 
the spherical flame shape enabled by the microgravity environment. Models include gas-phase 
and burner-surface radiation. 
 
Buoyant gravity-driven flow complicates the interpretation of the existing results and has led to 
different theories to explain the permanently-blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether this 
phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame, or to a 
change in the detailed structure of the flame. 
 
The challenges of normal-gravity studies are avoided by performing the tests on the International 
Space Station (ISS), where the non-buoyant microgravity flames allow the effects of convection 
direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel from the burner into 
an oxidizer (e.g., air) in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is 
unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer from the burner into an 
atmosphere of fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. 
 
Furthermore, microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide 
various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a 
buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in 
microgravity. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame 
structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, 
can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much 
stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than 
normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence 
times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames 
are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of 
limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages,

normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence 
times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames 
are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of 
limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, 
microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – 
regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
Flame Design should yield unique data that allows for a better understanding of how nitrogen 
exchange affects soot-inception and flame extinction, and how it can be used to design optimum 
flames. In addition, the effects of flow direction are also studied, and the importance of the flow 
direction and flame structure to permanently-blue flames is assessed.

II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
B. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
Flame Design and other ACME experiments were configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew. The crew’s role was to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of 
tests. The most common changes included the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All ACME testing was commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS 
Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of ACME testing was conducted 
in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. While it was possible to 
make some ‘manual’ changes outside of the script, e.g., to approach a flame’s soot limit, 
during a test that was not done in any ACME testing, neglecting minor exceptions, e.g., to 
terminate tests after the flames had extinguished. 
 
Testing was not conducted when thrusters fired or spacecraft docked or undocked from 
ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data was downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for 
preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 
 
 
III. Results 
G. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 326 flames were ignited for the Flame Design experiment during Increments 
59/50 and 66, where 188 and 138 flames were ignited in the two increments, respectively. 
 
The first-round tests featured normal flames, where gaseous fuel was ejected from a 
porous spherical burner into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. In contrast, the second 
round - except for its first test day - was carried out with inverse flames, in which the 
oxidizer is ejected from the burner into a fuel/nitrogen atmosphere. As a result, the 
second-round flames were ‘inside out.’ The ‘interruption’ in the Flame Design testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results 
in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific 
outcome. 
 
Flame Design did not have living subjects like a life science experiment, where the tests 
were conducted with the gaseous fuel ethylene (C2H4). It is a simple hydrocarbon gas for 
which the chemistry is well understood and it is typically highly sooting because of its 
carbon double bond. The tests were conducted with both pure fuel and fuel mixed with 
nitrogen. In the latter case, the ACME hardware allows for simultaneous flow of fuel

H. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
3. Mission anomalies 
There were no significant anomalies hindering Flame Design operations during 
Increments 59-60, but there was a pertinent anomaly that had previously occurred. 
It was discovered on 4 Feb. 2019 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas 
bottle for the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle 
had been on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a 
nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and 
not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was 
replaced on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration. 
 
On 27 Dec. 2021 (GMT 361), during Increment 66, it was determined that the Thin 
Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array was not aligned to the ACME Data Camera 
(DataCam) as intended, i.e., so that the fibers would be orthogonal relative to the 
camera. Unfortunately, this was the fourth day of testing in which the fiber array 
wasn’t aligned, where it regrettably wasn’t recognized earlier. Given the importance 
of the TFP-derived measurements of the flame temperature, testing was halted until 
the array was aligned (with other crew tasks) by Raja Chari on 17 Jan. 2022 (GMT 017). 
 
4. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data 
Flame Design tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software 
script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As 
a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. Such 
aborts normally occured because of communication issues with an Image Processing 
and Storage Unit (IPSU). These were infrequent, but there were some days when 
ACME tests aborted repeatedly. 
 
ACME tests were of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. In the first 
round of Flame Design testing, the igniter tip failed twice requiring crew time to be 
scheduled to replace it before the subsequent test day could be conducted. 
Regrettably, it was sometimes discovered during ACME testing that the igniter had 
failed during the final test of the preceding test day, where an example was on 10 
June 2019 (19161) when no flames were ignited as a result (as discussed in section 
III.A). An igniter check was subsequently added to the ACME end-of-test-day 
procedure to avoid such recurrences. However, on another test day, it was believed 
that the igniter tip had failed but ignition was instead prevented because the chamber 
pressure exceeded the pressure switch limit. Ignition was achieved after the chamber 
pressure was appropriately reduced.

I. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The 326 flames ignited in the two rounds of greatly exceeds the 76 tests which were 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD). As 
a result, more than 4.2 times as many flames were ignited than required. 
 
However, as discussed in Section III.A, the performance of the first spherical burner was 
not always satisfactory – where the flame was not always sufficiently spherical or 
centered on the burner, suggesting extreme asymmetry in the flow field and thus 
questionable data. Yet, 240 flames were ignited with the second burner, which is over 
3.1 times the number of required tests. 
 
ACME’s sintered spherical burners do not yield spherically symmetric flames which are 
centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical 
symmetry. This lack of symmetry was especially evident at high burner flows. It is very 
likely that the sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube is more porous than 
the sintered sphere itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supply tube. 
There was significant improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was 
replaced mid-way through round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003). But 
the symmetry is not perfect and this is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data. 
 
Portions of ACME’s recorded image data were sometimes deleted without downlinking. 
This was done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can 
be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision was sometimes made to 
sacrifice some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be 
conducted. This was intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each 
day of testing within the project constraints. 
 
The signal from the ACME radiometer array used in round 1 of Flame Design testing was 
saturated for nearly every test, yielding non-useful data. For round 2 of FLame Design, 
the radiometer array was replaced with the radiometer array designed for Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) which yielded satisfactory measurements. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually

K. Preliminary Research Findings 
Flame Design results have shown that spherical diffusion flames in microgravity have 
unique characteristics that are valuable for fundamental studies of diffusion flames. 
Flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen 
concentration. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size such that very small flames - just 
above their kinetic extinction limits - have low radiative loss, and asymptotically approach 
steady-state behavior. Larger flames increase in size over time until the rate of radiative 
heat loss becomes sufficiently large, and the flame extinguishes via radiative extinction. 
Before total extinction occurs in these flames, they experience an unstable, oscillatory 
mode, in which they partially extinguish and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude 
until total extinction. For constant ambient oxygen concentration, larger flames (with 
higher fuel flow rates) radiatively extinguish faster than smaller flames (with lower flow 
rates) due to higher radiative losses and decreasing chemical heat release. A thorough 
analysis of low flow rate flames was completed in order to investigate the existence of 
steady-state spherical flames, which has been a subject of debate in literature. It was 
found that steady state microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist. Furthermore, it 
was found that ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar extinguish at a 
critical extinction point defined by an extinction flame temperature and an extinction 
reactant mass flux at the flame.

Whether steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion exist in the 
presence of radiation heat loss is an important fundamental question and has 
important implications for spacecraft fire safety. In this work, experiments aboard

Gaseous spherical diffusion flames stabilized on a porous spherical burner are 
employed in normal (i.e., fuel flowing into an ambient oxidizer) and inverse (i.e., 
oxidizer flowing into an ambient fuel) flame configurations. The fuel is ethylene

gas from the burner is held constant. It is found that steady-state gaseous 
microgravity spherical diffusion flames do exist in the presence of radiation heat

radiative extinction, and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss

spherical, infinite domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusion -

steady-state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the 
constraint of a finite boundary. Steady-state flames are simulated using the

(i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure 
ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactant mass flow rate. Flame 
growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point 
is reached, is attributed to the natural development of a diffusion limited system 
as it approaches steady state and the dependence of transport properties on 
temperature as temperature is reduced by radiation (i.e., radiation-induced 
growth).

Week 8: April 26 – May 2 
On GMT 115, the first ACME Flame Design test points were performed. Pure gaseous ethylene fuel was 
ejected into air from a porous sphere, which, in microgravity, results in a one-dimensional, spherical 
flame. Thus, data analysis is greatly simplified because the flame shape doesn’t need to be predicted, and 
computational modeling can focus on the detailed chemistry and transport of the molecules and energy. 
 
The goal of Flame Design is to improve our understanding of soot processes so that flames can be 
“designed” to be soot free. This research could help lead to reduced soot and NOx—and thus reduced 
smog and acid rain—through nitrogen exchange, where the nitrogen is shifted from the air to the fuel. 
This oxygen-enriched combustion of diluted fuel could also facilitate carbon sequestration (i.e., capture 
and storage).

As can be seen in Figure 1, the flame is nominally spherical, but heat loss to the burner tube causes it to 
locally quench. Similarly, candle flames have an open gap close to the candle, again due to heat loss. These 
non-premixed flames are a bit like bubbles, where the flame is the shell where the fuel and oxygen 
combine and create heat, light, and chemical products like carbon dioxide and water. In premixed flames, 
the fuel is within the “bubble” and the oxygen is outside of it. Future Flame Design tests are planned 
where the flame will be inside out, i.e., inverted. To conduct those tests (planned for 2020), the CIR's 
Combustion Chamber will be filled with a fuel/nitrogen mixture while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture will 
flow from the burner. 
 
Week 9: May 3-9 
On GMT 123, 19 spherical flames were successfully ignited for ACME Flame Design. Gaseous ethylene 
fuel, typically diluted with nitrogen, was ejected into air from the porous sphere at the end of the 
burner. Compared to the test points on GMT 115, these tests were conducted with higher flow rates, 
which resulted in larger flames of shorter durations. 
 
In most of the tests, the harp-like array of 14-micron ceramic fibers was translated into the flame to 
determine the radial temperature distribution. Where a fiber is visibly glowing, the temperature can be 
determined from its color, where yellow is hotter than orange, which in turn is hotter than red. The 
ACME color camera was carefully characterized prior to launch enabling a quantitative determination of 
the temperature by comparison of the red, green, and blue color planes in a measurement technique 
referred to as pyrometry.

This sequence of preliminary monochrome flame images is a life history of an example Flame Design 
flame. 
(a) Shortly after ignition, the ignition-created soot is being carried out of the flame by the gas flow from 
the porous spherical burner. 
(b) The amount of soot has decreased dramatically and the blue flame (neglecting the bright spots of the 
soot particulate) has expanded and dimmed. Since the fuel is inside the flame and oxygen is outside, the 
flame expands outward until it reaches enough oxygen to consume the fuel. The gas flow is outward from 
the burner sphere, so the oxygen must diffuse inward due to its concentration gradient. That gradient, 
and thus the oxygen transport, diminishes (i.e., flattens) with time due to both the oxygen consumption 
and the release of combustion byproducts like carbon dioxide and water vapor. A flame becomes 
effectively blanketed by these byproducts, inhibiting the oxygen transport. 
(c) The visible soot has mostly disappeared, and the flame has further grown and dimmed. The base of 
the flame has retreated from the burner tube because of heat loss. 
(d) The fiber array has begun translating with the first ceramic fiber at the edge of flame, where its glow 
is visible at the top of the image. Again, the soot continued to disappear, and the flame continued to grow 
and retreat from the burner tube. 
(e) Two fibers are in the flame and the third is close enough to visibly glow. The flame is a shell, where the 
fibers are cooler (i.e., dimmer in this gray-scale image) within the flame. A comparison of images (d) and 
(e) reveals that the flame base is oscillating, which is a sign of approaching extinction. 
(f) The flame has nearly extinguished due to radiative heat loss and is very faint in comparison to the 
earlier images. The fibers are dimmer in image (f) than (e), indicating the decrease in flame temperature.

While Flame Design’s primary objective is to determine the conditions under which flames are soot-free 
or soot producing, a secondary objective is to establish flammability limits for these spherical flames. We 
have observed interesting phenomena where the flames sometimes self-extinguish after growing 
oscillations. These oscillations are apparent in the above graph, which shows the chemiluminescence from 
excited molecules that drop to a lower energy state by emitting a photon at a specific wavelength. CH* 
chemiluminescence is the source of most of the blue seen in hydrocarbon flames and OH* 
chemiluminescence is in the ultraviolet. These two measurements are made with Photomultipiler Tubes 
(PMTs), where each tube is equipped with a narrow-band filter corresponding to an excited molecule. 
 
In the example shown in the graph, the flame’s oscillations lasted about 30 seconds and occurred at 
roughly 1 Hz, but they slowed in frequency as they grew in strength. The oscillations are evident in the 
imaging, where the flame locally quenches—creating a hole in the flame. This hole allows for increased 
mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which in turn results in a recovery of the flame. The size of the opening in 
the flame (which normally separates the fuel and oxygen) grows with time until the entire flame 
extinguishes. 
 
Interestingly, the graph shows that the CH* measurement was relatively steady before the start of the 
oscillations in comparison with the decaying OH* emission. This difference will be further examined to 
improve our understanding of flame extinction.

CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
This test point video shows a sooty flame, and, in the absence of buoyancy, the soot stays within 
the flame and clusters. Some of the glowing soot clusters move out of the flame due to the 
outward flow of the diluted ethylene fuel through the burner’s porous sphere. In contrast, some 
of the clusters get trapped within the flame due to a temperature gradient that moves them 
inward toward the cold burner and away from the hot flame. 
 
After some time, the harp-like array of 14-micron ceramic fibers is translated into the flame to 
determine the radial temperature distribution. Using a carefully characterized camera, the 
temperature can be quantitatively determined from a glowing fiber’s color, where yellow is hotter 
than orange, and orange is hotter than red. The motion of the fiber arm causes the soot clusters 
to move away from the fibers. 
 
While the temperature measurements are being made, the flow of diluted ethylene is gradually 
reduced, which causes the flame to become smaller and unstable. Heat loss causes the flame to 
locally quench—creating a hole in the flame near the burner tube. This hole allows for increased 
mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which reinvigorates the flame and causes it to close again. The 
flame opens and closes, effectively consuming fuel in repeated gulps…a bit like a video-game 
character eating dots. But as the fuel flow is reduced further, the size of the open “mouth” gets 
smaller, as if the flame is becoming full. The flame becomes stable again until the flow becomes 
so small that the flame finally goes out. 
 
This video illustrates the extreme complexities of even conceptually simple flames! Even though 
mankind has been using combustion for millennia, microgravity research can unlock new 
understanding, which would lead to improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in 
practical terrestrial combustion.

Week 3: Oct. 29 – Nov. 4 
On GMT 301, we began the second round of testing for ACME Flame Design with 18 normal flames ignited 
using propane fuel. The goal of Flame Design is to improve our understanding of soot processes so that 
flames can be “designed” to be soot free. The remaining tests will look at inverse flames, which are formed 
when diluted oxygen flows from the burner into a Combustion Chamber filled with diluted fuel. Compared 
to normal flames, inverse flames are inside out so soot is formed outside rather than inside the flame. 
While soot processes are known to depend on flame temperature and the residence time of the fuel at 
high temperatures, a comparison of normal- and inverse-flame results will help us better understand the 
impact of flow direction on soot processes. On GMT 306 and 307, Shane Kimbrough, Megan McArthur 
and Mark Vande Hei configured the ACME Chamber Insert and replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold 
#2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support the inverse flame tests for Flame Design Part 2. 
 
 
Figure 1. Flame Design Normal Propane Flame 
 
This false-colored image of a soot-free spherical flame shows an array of 14-micron ceramic fibers making 
temperature measurements. The blue in the image has been enhanced so that the dim flame is visible in 
addition to the fibers. Normally, the hot fibers appear to be red, orange, and yellow—in order of increasing 
temperature—just like metal in a forge. The temperature profile along each fiber is optically determined 
from its varying hue through a technique known as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). 
 
The base of the flame has locally quenched due to heat loss to the burner’s supply tube, which created a 
hole in the flame. This hole allowed for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which enhanced flammability 
and causes the flame to momentarily reform. In this test, the spherical flame repeatedly opened and 
closed with oscillations that grew in strength until the entire flame extinguished.

Week 7: Nov. 26 – Dec. 2 
On GMT 328, we ignited nine inverse flames for ACME Flame Design. For these tests, an oxygen/nitrogen 
mixture flowed from the burner into a combustion chamber, which was filled with an ethylene/nitrogen 
mixture. For one of these tests, we observed our longest sustained flame, which burned for over 14 
minutes. At that time, operational constraints required its termination. For comparison, flame durations 
for all ACME experiments are typically shorter than two minutes with the longest—until now—under six 
minutes. This 14+ minute flame has led to new understanding of the stability of spherical flames. 
 
While test measurements did show that this long-duration flame was slowly weakening with time, it might 
have burned significantly longer. We have found with higher burner flow rates that flames grow with time 
and extinguish due to radiative heat loss. If the flow rate is too low, the flame’s small size leads to excessive 
burner heating. But under the right conditions, the flame can burn for minutes and perhaps even tens of 
minutes.

This false-colored image was taken about halfway through the 14+ minute test. The blue in the image has 
been enhanced so that the dim flame is visible in addition to the ceramic fiber, which is glowing at the top 
of the flame. We use the fibers for optical determination of the flame’s temperature.

In this test point video, we translated the 14-micron ceramic fibers into the flame to optically

Figure 1. Effect of Pressure on Flame Design Inverse Flames 
 
This composite image shows the effect of chamber pressure on inverse flames. Although the pressure 
didn't greatly affect the size of the flames, it still had a significant effect. The flame at lower pressure is 
much brighter because at higher pressures light-emitting molecules are more likely to be extinguished 
due to molecular collisions. Also, the low-pressure flame shows subtle signs of soot formation. At the top 
of the flame, the blue edge is tinted with yellow due to soot, which also creates a haze just above the 
flame. Inverse flames are inside out, where the soot is formed outside of the flame when the hot fuel 
combines with itself in the absence of oxygen (which is inside the flame). The porous spherical burner is 
illuminated in red from the illumination package we sometimes use during imaging.

Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The Flame Design data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where that is generally 
true for the ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples 
that were subsequently transported to the ground. 
 
The Flame Design image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, used at least generally with a CH* filter 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package 
 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format as well as a converted Tagged Image 
File (tif) format. NASA’s post-processing of the raw images was carried out without each of the following: 
a. color balancing (to avoid possible saturation) 
b. dark frame subtraction 
c. removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage) 
Furthermore, the conversion employed a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is detrimental 
when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) because it will average pixels 
both on and off the glowing fibers. 
 
The images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are provided in a tif format. Meanwhile, the analog 
operations (ops) video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was used during a limited number of Flame 
Design test days and the resulting raw data files are in a text (i.e., ASCII) format. 
 
Consult the forthcoming ACME/Flame Design Data Interpretation document to learn more. 
 
The raw Flame Design data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available 
publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

administrators with success in patents, licensing, and commercialization and have produced 
technologies that have brought or aspire to bring, real impact on the welfare of society. They are 
rising stars who foster a spirit of innovation within their communities and institutions while educating 
and mentoring the next generation of inventors.” As explained in his university’s press release and 
department’s 2022 brochure about this honor, “Axelbaum holds 10 patents and founded the startup 
company AP Material Inc., which commercialized a flame-synthesis technology to manufacture high-
purity nanopowders.”

NASA Project Scientist Dennis Stocker created the Space Flames Facebook page 
(www.facebook.com/space.flames) and Flickr site (https://www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames),

Task Description:
NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion
Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of
Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A). 
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. 
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at
NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and
computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter
Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland. 
 
Rationale for HRP Directed Research: 
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants. 
 
Task Progress:
We have completed Round 1 (normal flames) and Round 2 (inverse flames) of Flame Design testing and are processing
and analyzing the data. We are running Sphdif simulations and publishing the findings. 
Three journal papers were published this year and one other was submitted. One conference paper was published and
presented. Kendyl Waddell defended and published his Ph.D. dissertation. 
Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San
Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. We
simulated ethylene flames to perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state
flames.

February 2024 Update per PI. See Bibliography for additional information. (Ed., 2/15/24) Despite a range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical temperature of 1130 K, a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. With this information, we have developed a simple equation to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactant mass flow rate. Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth). dilution ratio measurement. A high flow rate of dilution N2 (~45 SLPM) is applied and the dilution ratio is controlled to
a range of 30 – 200. The probe samples the whole particle stream while maintaining quasi-isokinetic sampling, and is

Based on recent findings, the new graduate student at Washington University is beginning to construct a tri-coflow
burner to test a theory of applying Flame Design concepts to control heat flux. We have modified an existing burner to
create a triaxial coflow flame. The inner nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air, the middle nozzle supplies fuel
(methane) or nitrogen diluted fuel, and the outer nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air. The inner oxidizer creates an
inner flame sheet, resulting in two distinct flame zones. The goal of this project is to maximize radiation heat transfer in
methane combustion by using flame design concepts to create a soot favorable environment at the inner flame sheet and
then oxidize soot particles before they are released to the ambient environment. We have been taking high speed videos
of the flame sheet interactions and are preparing to take radiation measurements.

Wendong Wu successfully defended his Ph.D. in May, 2017, at Washington University in St. Louis. The collaboration
between Washington University and Shanghai Jiaotong University will continue in the field of laser plasma diagnostics.
Graduate student Pan Du has joined the Flame Design team. 
At the University of Maryland, we continue to examine the effects of dilution on lengths of normal and inverse gas jet
diffusion flames. The method of measuring flame lengths was refined to examine only the blue intensities in the recorded
images. Both normal and inverse flames now correlate together according to the theory of Roper. We have also
characterized the double flame structure visible in some inverse diffusion flames. We imaged the double flames at 310
and 430 nm. We are measuring oxygen concentrations and temperatures in and above the double flames. This will help
to determine if oxygen in this region contributes to the formation of the double luminous zones. A paramagnetic oxygen
analyzer is being used, which has a mole fraction range of 0-1 and an accuracy of 0.001%. 
At the University of Hawaii Manoa, Beei-Huan Chao has retired and resigned from his role as Flame Design
Co-Investigator. His invaluable contributions to Flame Design are greatly appreciated and will be missed going forward.
Prior to his retirement, progress was made on analytical studies of C/O ratio in diffusion flames. We examined extinction
of spherical diffusion flames attached to a burner and revisited reactant leakage of diffusion flames. We revisited
Linan's 1974 paper following the “total enthalpy” concept.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A). 
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the Principal Investigator, the three Co-Investigators, and staff at NASA
Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and
computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, Peter Sunderland
directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland (UMD), and Beei-Huan Chao directing analytical work and
computations at University of Hawaii.

in Diffusion Flames, Combustion
and Flame, accepted. The kinetic behavior of the water-gas-shift (WGS) sub-system has been studied computationally
for hydrocarbon diffusion flames in the counterflow geometry. Of specific interest was the spatial domain in which the
reactions in the WGS-complex exhibit characteristics that lead to species concentrations approaching those expected
from equilibrium. Two scenarios were observed for WGS equilibrium: 
(1) Full equilibrium in which every step of the WGS-mechanism is nearly in equilibrium; 
(2) “Apparent” equilibrium, which is achieved via opposing but coherent shifts away from equilibrium for the two key
elementary reactions that constitute the WGS reaction. This interesting phenomenon is caused by the supply of the H
radical, which participates in the forward reaction of one step and the reverse reaction of the other. This new form of
apparent equilibrium differs from well-known “quasi” equilibrium, which is typically caused by the combination of a
fast reversible step and slow irreversible step. 
Parametric domains where found in which these two scenarios are observed. For a given fuel type it was shown that the
two scenarios can be separated by the location of stoichiometry. On the oxidizer side, full equilibrium of the overall
WGS reaction is achieved, while on the fuel side, apparent equilibrium can occur. 
Z. Wang, M. El Makawy, P.B. Sunderland, B. Chao, R.L. Axelbaum, The Effects of Reactant Dilution on Lengths of
Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Many past studies have examined the
stoichiometric lengths of laminar gas jet diffusion flames. These are found to be independent of pressure and burner
diameter for fixed fuel mass flow rate. However, some studies report flame lengths increase when inert is added to the

fuel stream, whereas others report no change. Furthermore, measurements of effects of inert in the ambient gas are
sparse, as are measurements for inverse flames. The analytical model of Roper (CNF 29:219, 1977) accounts for the full
range of reactant dilution and inverse flames, but has only been tested for fuel-air systems. 
This work examines the stoichiometric lengths of normal and inverse steady methane/oxygen/nitrogen jet flames burning
on a 3.0 mm coflowing burner inside a glass chimney. Nitrogen dilution is such that methane mole fractions vary from
0.15 – 1 and oxygen mole fractions vary from 0.18 – 1. The measured flame lengths vary from 3 – 53 mm.
Stoichiometric lengths are measured from visible emissions of the blue flame sheets. Reactant flow rates are measured
with calibrated rotameters. 
The predictions of the Roper model are compared with the measured flame lengths. For normal flames the agreement is
best for a mass diffusivity at 25 C of 17 mm2/s and a temperature of 0.94 times the adiabatic flame temperature. This
contrasts to values used by Roper for methane/air flames of 20 mm2/s and 1500 K, respectively. For the present
conditions the predictions match the measurements with a R2 coefficient of determination of 0.91. 
For fixed fuel flow rate, inert addition to the fuel stream is found to increase flame length, but this effect is negligible for
fuel mole fractions above 0.5. 
A simplified approximation of the Roper model has been obtained for normal methane/nitrogen/oxygen diffusion
flames. This removes the requirement to specify adiabatic flame temperature and stoichiometric mixture fraction. The
simplified model predicts flame length from the methane flow rate and mole fraction and the oxygen mole fraction. 
W. Wu, R.L. Axelbaum, Interpreting Flame Structure by Mixture Fraction Measurement Using Laser-Induced
Breakdown Spectroscopy, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Measuring mixture fractions in a broad range of
combustion systems with a suitable spatial and temporal resolution is critical not only for understanding the flame
behavior, but also for the validation of rapidly developing numerical models. Instead of deriving the mixture fraction
from measured molecular profile, a new approach of obtaining such quantities from atomic ratios measured by laser
induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is introduced in this study. The atomic ratios for C, N, H, and O (e.g., C/O,
H/O, and N/O) for the LIBS system were first calibrated in an ethylene-air premixed flat flame, where the equivalence
ratio of the pre-mixture was varied from 0.60 to 1.80. Then the atomic ratio distributions along the centerline of an
ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame were measured to demonstrate the capability of LIBS to measure atomic ratios
between different elements throughout the entire flame. The elemental mass fractions for C, H, N, O can be thus
obtained from atomic ratio profiles.

Flame Design is a spaceflight combustion experiment that will examine several unusual aspects of spherical diffusion
flames fueled by gases. Its emphasis is on soot formation and flame extinction. This experiment, and associated
ground-based work, attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent
constraints, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This presentation will introduce the
overall concepts of Flame Design. It will summarize observations in the NASA Glenn 2.2 s and 5 s drop facilities,
which have yielded important insights into soot formation and flame extinction behavior. Detailed numerical modeling
of spherical diffusion flames have aided the understanding of the observations. Recent advances in Laser-Induced
Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) will be discussed. LIBS allows the C/O atom ratio to be measured in flames. This
diagnostic is well suited to use in spaceflight experiments.

Task Description:
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The
division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington
University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, Peter Sunderland directing numerical simulations
at University of Maryland, and Beei-Huan Chao directing analytical work and computations at University of Hawaii. 
 
Rationale for HRP Directed Research: 
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants. 
 
Task Progress:
Summary of Accomplishments: 
• The research team published 4 peer-reviewed journal articles during this period. This work is summarized below. 
• Work at Washington University continued to pursue normal gravity experiments of soot formation in diffusion flames,
numerical modeling, and chemical kinetics. 
• Work at Univ. of Maryland continued to pursue numerical models of spherical diffusion flames, including soot
formation and extinction. 
• Work at Univ. of Hawaii continued to pursue analytical and computational studies of soot formation, radiation, and
extinction in diffusion flames. 
• The flight experiment was supported in various ways. For example, the research team responded to issues raised by
NASA engineers in refining the test matrix and ACME requirements document. The research team also aided staff at
NASA Glenn with burner characterization drop testing in the 5 s drop facility.

V.R. Lecoustre, P.B. Sunderland, B.H. Chao, R.L. Axelbaum, Modeled Quenching Limits of Spherical Hydrogen
Diffusion Flames, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 34 (2013) 887-894. Hydrogen-air diffusion flames were
modeled with an emphasis on kinetic extinction. The flames were one-dimensional spherical laminar diffusion flames
supported by adiabatic porous burners of various diameters. Behavior of normal (H2 flowing into quiescent air) and
inverse (air flowing into quiescent H2) configurations were considered using detailed H2/O2 chemistry and transport
properties with updated light component diffusivities. For the same heat release rate, inverse flames were found to be
smaller and 290 K hotter than normal flames. The weakest normal flame that could be achieved before quenching has an
overall heat release rate of 0.25 W, compared to 1.4 W for the weakest inverse flame. There is extensive leakage of the
ambient reactant for both normal and inverse flames near extinction, which results in a premixed flame regime for
diffusion flames except for the smallest burners with radii on the order of 1 micron. At high flow rates
H+OH(+M)?H2O(+M) contributes over 40% of the net heat release. However at flow rates approaching quenching
limits, H+O2(+M)?HO2(+M) is the elementary reaction with the largest heat release rate. The corresponding author for
this paper was P.B. Sunderland. 
F. Xia, R.L. Axelbaum, Simplifying the complexity of diffusion flames through interpretation in C/O ratio space,
Computers and Mathematics with Applications, 65 (2013) 1625-1632. Understanding the structure of diffusion flames is
often complicated by the dependence of flame structure on the boundary conditions, e.g. composition, temperature and
flow field (e.g., strain rate in a counterflow flame.) In this paper, the local carbon-to-oxygen atom ratio (C/O ratio) is
applied as a variable to interpret the flame and soot zone structures of counterflow diffusion flames from numerical
results with detailed chemical kinetics and transport. Radical pool and soot precursor zones are shown to be clearly
delineated in C/O ratio space. The boundary of these two zones, as well as the flame location, are shown to be
independent of both stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) and strain rate when interpreted in C/O space. The kinetic ratio
is used to study the characteristics of key chemical reactions and to identify regions of equilibrium for these reactions.
The results of this paper indicate that the C/O ratio is a valuable variable for interpreting flame structure and soot
precursor chemistry for diffusion flames. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.

F. Xia, G.S. Yablonsky, R.L. Axelbaum, Numerical Study of Flame Structure and Soot Inception Interpreted in
Carbon-to-Oxygen Atom Ratio Space, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 1085-1091. The utility of
interpreting flame results in carbon-to-oxygen atom ratio (C/O ratio) space, as opposed to physical space or mixture
fraction space, is evaluated. Flame and soot zone structures of counterflow diffusion flames have been studied for C2H4
and C3H8 and interpreted in C/O ratio space as a function of stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst). The
Burke-Schumann results expressed in C/O ratio space demonstrate how a clear and direct understanding of how
structure is affected by Zst can be realized in C/O ratio space because, unlike physical or mixture fraction space, the
flame location is independent of stoichiometric mixture fraction. Numerical results with detailed chemical kinetics also
indicate that C/O ratio space is a fundamental variable in the sense that, for a given fuel, the location of the flame zones
and critical reactions is invariant with Zst and strain rate. Two zones are clearly observed, namely the radical pool and
the soot precursor zone located on the fuel side of the flame. The onset threshold of soot precursors (C6H5 and C6H6)
for the high temperature side of the soot precursor zone is characterized by the depletion of radicals. The role of the
hydrogen radical in flame structure and soot inception is demonstrated by studying its production and consumption
channels in C/O ratio space. Finally, a modified (C/O)* is given to interpret the physical meaning of C/O ratio. The
numerical results in this work indicate and explain the advantages of applying C/O ratio space in the analysis of flame
structure and soot precursor chemistry. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum. 
F. Yi, R.L. Axelbaum, Stability of Spray Combustion for Water/Alcohols Mixtures in Oxygen-Enriched Air,
Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 1697-1704. The feasibility of burning fuels that are heavily diluted
with water was evaluated. This concept could potentially be utilized to directly generate steam for a variety of
applications, including power generation and enhanced oil recovery. Two water-soluble fuels, ethanol and 1-propanol,

were heavily diluted with water and sprayed into a swirl-stabilized burner and the blow-off limits were obtained to
identify the flame stability. The blow-off limit was experimentally determined as the lowest O2 concentration where a
flame could exist under a given oxidizer flow rate. For the present experimental system, stability maps were determined
as a function of fuel concentration and oxidizer flow rate for different types of nozzles and both alcohols. Contours of
temperature and overall fuel mass fraction in the droplets were obtained for a flame burning 15 wt% ethanol in an
oxidizer of 50% O2 and 50% N2. The results revealed that preferential vaporization of ethanol over water plays an
important role in enhancing flame stability. To further understand this, a model of bi-component droplet vaporization
was employed for both the diffusion limit and distillation limit modes of liquid mass transfer. The results confirmed the
preferential vaporization of ethanol and demonstrated that it is necessary to account for the non-ideal solution behavior
of the alcohol-water mixture to appropriately model the vaporization process. The model also demonstrated that for this
experimental system, droplet vaporization was better characterized by the distillation limit mode with enhanced mass
transfer by convection. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.

Task Description:
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. 
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The
division of labor is roughly broken up with PBS and DLU performing microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn
Research Center, PBS directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland, BHC performing analytical work and
computations at University of Hawaii, and RLA performing normal gravity experiments and computations at
Washington University.

Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For
example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

Task Progress:
The following is a summary of the research activities during the period Oct. 2006 - Sept. 2009. 
1) Numerical and Experimental Observations of Spherical Diffusion Flames. Spherical diffusion flames supported on a
porous sphere were studied numerically and experimentally. Experiments were performed in 2.2 s and 5.2 s microgravity
facilities. Numerical results were obtained from a Chemkin-based program. The program simulates flow from a porous
sphere into a quiescent environment, yields both steady state and transient results and accounts for optically thick
gas-phase radiation. The low flow velocities and long residence times in these diffusion flames lead to enhanced radiative
and diffusive effects. Despite similar adiabatic flame temperatures, the measured and predicted temperatures varied by as
much as 700 K. The temperature reduction correlates with flame size but characteristic flow times and Lewis number
also influence temperature. The numerical results show that the ambient gas Lewis number would have a strong effect
on flame temperature if the flames were steady and nonradiating. For example, a 10% decrease in Lewis number would
increase the steady state flame temperature by 200 K. However, for these transient, radiating flames the effect of Lewis
number is small. It was also observed that when hydrocarbon fuel is supplied from the ambient the large diffusion
distances associated with these flames can lead to unusual steady state compositions near the outer boundary because
decomposition products can diffuse to the outer boundary. This results in a loss of chemical enthalpy from the system
but the effect on flame temperature is small. Transient predictions of flame sizes are larger than those observed in
microgravity experiments. Close agreement could not be obtained without either increasing the model’s thermal and
mass diffusion properties by 30% or reducing mass flowrate by 25%.

diffusion flames was investigated experimentally and numerically. The experiments involved microgravity spherical

this work is that while radiative heat losses can drive transient extinction, this is not only because radiative losses are
increasing with time but also because the heat release rate is falling off as the flame expands away from the burner and
the reactant supply to the flame decreases.

inception region is shown to be bounded by two isotherms: a low-temperature boundary that is a function of residence

effect of increasing Zst is to move the boundaries of the soot inception zone towards each other, until the zone is
infinitely thin and thus the sooting limit is reached. By comparing the model to experimental data, a critical local C/O
ratio of 0.53 and a sooting limit inception temperature of 1640 K (for a characteristic residence time of 22 ms) were
determined for ethylene.

2) A new numerical study of limiting conditions for soot particle inception in spherical diffusion flames has been
initiated. The flames were modeled using a one-dimensional, time accurate diffusion flame code with detailed chemistry
and transport and an optically thick radiation model. Seventeen normal and inverse flames were considered, covering a
wide range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature, and residence time. These flames were
previously observed to reach their sooting limits after 2 s of microgravity. Sooting-limit diffusion flames with residence
times longer than 200 ms were found to have temperatures near 1190 K where C/O = 0.6, whereas flames with shorter
residence times required increased temperatures. Acetylene was found to be a reasonable surrogate for soot precursor
species in these flames, having peak mole fractions of about 0.01. 
3) Our previous studies have shown a linear relationship between the limit flame temperature and stoichiometric
mixture fraction for coflow flames at their sooting limit. The sooting limit in coflow flames is obtained by varying the
amount of inert gas until soot appears above a predefined height. In this work sooting limits based on particle luminosity
were measured as a function of Zst. For each limit flame, the flame temperature was measured and defined as the limit
flame temperature. The limit flame temperature increases linearly with Zst, for both normal and inverse flames. The
effects of residence time have also been investigated, and the soot inception temperature was found to be dependent on
fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configuration. Earlier experimental results and modeling indicated
that a critical carbon to oxygen (C/O) ratio exists in the fuel rich region of the flame where soot inception is no longer
favorable due to the presence of oxygen containing species. We extended this model to include the effects of finite rate
chemistry and thus residence time on the sooting limit. This involved considering two boundaries for the soot inception
zone, one dictated by the C/O ratio and the other by the finite rate chemistry of fuel pyrolysis and soot inception. By
combining these two boundaries, a simple model was developed that describes how a sooting limit is attained. By
utilizing measured limit temperature data with the model we found the limit inception temperature for soot formation to
be 1640 K and the critical carbon to oxygen ratio to be 0.53. 
4) Performed analytical analysis of the kinetic and radiative extinction limits of a steady spherical diffusion flame
supported by a porous burner. A single step, overall and irreversible reaction that follows high activation energy
Arrhenius kinetics was adopted to describe the reaction rate. An optically thin radiation model was used to describe the
radiative heat loss. The kinetic and radiative extinction limits were observed from the analysis.

Task Description:
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to: 
1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame
front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane
flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature; 
2. Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue
flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame temperature,
size, color and soot volume fraction; 
3. Obtain extinction limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction, amount of inert and pressure
for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding extinction temperature; 
4. Evaluate whether this flame system can be used to obtain a pseudo-flammability limit for non-premixed flames in
terms of stoichiometric mixture fraction and amount of inert. If so, determine these limits for ethylene and methane
flames. Soot formation and flame extinction are problems of great concern in practical combustors. Recent
normal-gravity experiments using counterflow diffusion flames have shown that permanently-blue flames (which are
devoid of soot regardless of strain rate) and extinction-resistant flames can be produced for many hydrocarbon fuels by
nitrogen exchange (increased stoichiometric mixture fraction). Furthermore, there is a unique stoichiometric mixture
fraction wherein the flame temperature at extinction can be up to 200 K lower and the strain rate up to four times greater
than that for the standard hydrocarbon/air flame with the same flame temperature. The present experiments employ
microgravity conditions to allow for a unique set of experiments to clarify the underlying mechanisms responsible for
flame response to stoichiometric mixture fraction.

As the goal of this program is to develop an understanding of combustion with the aim of reducing pollutants and

present interest in carbon sequestration via oxygen-enriched combustion the present work is of particular importance as
it identifies methods of controlling a number of pollutants through oxygen-enriched combustion. 
 
Task Progress:
Below is a summary of the progress on this project for the year ending January 1, 2006: 
Flame Design benefited from several analytical and computational advances in 2005. These have yielded important
insight into many experimental observations by this project. This has laid the groundwork for two journal publications,
one which was submitted and one which is nearing submission. 
Work on the general behavior of spherical diffusion flames has demonstrated that a detailed transient numerical model
(with detailed chemistry, transport, and radiation) can predict flame size and flame temperature for microgravity
spherical diffusion flames. A simplified model indicates that Lewis number can have a large effect on flame temperature
for microgravity diffusion flames. This work has been submitted to the Combustion Symposium. 
Work on radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames has demonstrated that the detailed transient model can predict
extinction times for microgravity spherical diffusion flames. The work identified several scaling relationship for
extinguishing diffusion flames. This work is being finalized for an upcoming journal submission. 
A Nikon D100 color digital still camera has been configured for use in the 2.2 second drop tower. This provides four
images per drop. The images have 6 megapixels and 12 x 3 bit depth and are among the highest-fidelity images ever
recorded in the drop tower. 
This camera has been used to record images of 15 micron SiC fibers in flames in the 2.2 second drop tower. This has
yielded qualitative thin-filament pyrometry results for extinguishing spherical diffusion flames. Eighteen successful drop
tests were performed in the 2.2 second drop tower.

Testing in the 2.2-second drop tower has yielded sooting limits of spherical microgravity diffusion flames reacting
ethylene and oxygen at various levels of dilution. The results provide a quantitative comparison of the effects on
sooting limits of stoichiometric mixture fraction and convection direction. Testing in the drop tower also has identified
a number of extinction limits. 
Normal-gravity tests involving coflowing gas jet flames have considered a similar range of stoichiometric mixture
fraction for both normal and inverse conditions. These results lend support to the microgravity observations. 
Analytical modeling has advanced the understanding of the steady-state temperature, size, and residence times of the
present spherical flames. 
Numerical modeling, which incorporates detailed chemistry and transport, has lent insight into the effects of radiation
and unsteadiness of the present spherical flames. 
These results have been and are being disseminated in the publications listed in the publication section.

INTRODUCTION 
 
Science Summary 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under 
development with a set of five independent experiments which are each focused on advancing 
combustion technology through fundamental research. Four of the current ACME experiments 
are specifically directed at addressing energy and environmental concerns, while the fifth 
experiment addresses fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. The overall goals are to improve 
our understanding of materials flammability, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both 
optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, flame stability and extinction limits, 
soot control and reduction, oxygen enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon 
sequestration, and the use of electric fields for combustion control. 
 
While distinct, the ACME experiments share several significant traits. The principal unifying 
feature of the experiments is their use of gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than 
liquid or solid fuels. With this in common, the experiments will be conducted within the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) through the use of a single modular insert. In addition to the 
fuel state, the current set of ACME experiments all use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) 
flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are either one or two dimensional, 
depending upon the experiment. 
 
With the exception of the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment discussed immediately 
below, the general goal of the current ACME experiments is to gain fundamental understanding 
that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on 
Earth, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and 
transport processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced performance, 
improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design. 
In summary, microgravity investigations of non-premixed flames could lead to eco-friendly 
combustion systems providing our nation with green power for the future. 
 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) 
Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is 
focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraf t. Specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve 
our fundamental understanding of materials flamma bility, such as extinction behavior and the 
conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability 
test methods for low and partial-gravity envir onments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous 
fuel will simulate the burning of solid and liqui d fuels, where measurements are made of the 
thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon whic h the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels 
depend.

Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) 
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our 
current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, 
namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. The general goal of 
the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame 
conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical 
kinetic and soot formation submodels. The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection 
velocity and fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly 
sooting conditions. Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene 
flames in an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be directly applicable 
to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result 
of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the 
flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant 
emission. The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD 
Flames) experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and 
investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames. Outside reviewers 
concluded that the experiment “… will contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge 
of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted 
with a simple gas-jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage 
(up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) 
the burner. Measurements, as a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of the 
ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
Flame Design 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot 
inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the 
“design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. An outside review panel 
declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient 
and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and 
extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame 
experiment.

and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and 
extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame 
experiment. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene 
or methane) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot 
inception. The effect of the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both 
normal flames and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from 
the spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will explore 
whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for 
non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for 
premixed flames.

Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) 
The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment is to 
advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free 
and sooty flames. The spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity, will be created 
through use of a porous spherical burner from which a fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the 
CIR chamber. Flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition 
naturally toward extinction. Tests will be conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel 
and chamber atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane for soot-free flames, 
and ethylene for sooty flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for 
both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, 
respectively). Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating 
instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent 
mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

1.4.9. The burner shall have a uniform flow profile that is axisymmetric, i.e., where the 
velocity is independent of the angular position, especially (at radial positions) 
near the burner center. For the coflow bur ner, axisymmetric flow means that the 
variation in axial velocity with angular position (e.g., as measured in 1.4.11) shall 
be less than 10% of the (mean) velocit y, where this shall hold for all radial 
positions from 0 to 10 mm. For example, the axial velocities measured on the 
two sides (i.e., left and right) of a diameter shall match within 10% of the (mean) 
axial velocity at the same radial distance. The burner gas shall be ejected parallel 
to the chamber axis and without either swirl (i.e., helically rotating flow) or 
turbulence (i.e., eddies). To be without turbulence, the axial velocity at any 
position 0.5 mm downstream of the burner (e .g., as measured in 1.4.11) shall be 
constant with time within 3% (i.e ., of the time-averaged value). The use of

1.10. Ignition 
While hot-wire igniters have been effectivel y used in many combustion experiments, 
special care is required for ACME because of the testing with elevated oxygen (for 
the Flame Design experiment) which leads to higher flame temperatures which in 
turn could significantly shorten igniter life . Hot Surface Ignition (HSI), which is 
often used in furnaces, may be better for ACME than hot-wire ignition. 
1.10.1. The igniter shall reliably ignite all initia l flow conditions. Reliable ignition shall 
be verified in 1g at the limiting (i.e., extreme) conditions in the test matrices for 
each burner within 1 s of igniter activation. For the spherical and BRE burners, 
it is suggested that the ignition occur at about 3 mm from the burner outlet. For 
the gas-jet, coflow, and BRE burners, the i gnition should occur within the mixing 
layer between the fuel and oxidizer (and not centered on the burner axis).3,4,* 
1.10.2. Hydrodynamic disturbance from igniter insertion and retraction shall be 
minimized by inserting the igniter at least 30 s prior to ignition, and removing it 
from the free area within 0.5 s after igniti on detection. The igniter retraction time 
is a required example, where it shall be po ssible to vary that time as described in 
ACME’s Science Operations Requirements Document (SORD). The disturbance 
can be minimized through a linear rath er than a sweeping retraction, and by 
limiting the speed of the retraction (because a rapid retraction could disturb the 
flame). 
1.10.3. The igniter energy output shall be variable and minimized to ensure minimal 
effects on subsequent flame behavior and avoid igniter burnout. As one example 
of implementation, the igniter should not be energized longer than required.3,* 
1.10.4. The capability to vary the ignition dura tion and set it to an uplinked value 
between 0 and 10 s is required.*

4.1. CLD Flame 
The main goal of this experiment is to eva luate flame characteristics at the extremes 
of fuel dilution: both weak, highly-dilute flames, and sooting flames up to pure-fuel 
conditions. While such parameters as the extin ction limits and potential smoke points 
within these flames can easily be determin ed in normal gravity, we will not know the 
exact microgravity limits until the experiment is run on the ISS. We therefore plan to 
execute an initial run for each fuel where we vary the flow velocities and dilution 
levels in order to determine the extinc tion limits and degree of soot production in 
microgravity. For extinction limits, the flow velocity will be slowly ramped until 
extinction is observed for a given dilution level. The dilution level will then be 
increased in 5% increments and the proce dure repeated. Extinction can be detected 
quickly with a PMT, but the color imagi ng system, HiBMs camera, and ops imaging 
system will all be run during these scans to maximize the data collected. For sooting 
determination, the dilution level will be decr eased in 5% increments and/or the flow 
velocity will be increased in 5 cm/s in crements until soot is observed, and then 
continued until either a smoke point is reached or a predetermined upper limit is 
reached. These observations can be made using the ops and color imaging systems.

flames as well as identify any smoke points for the C 2H4 flames. Based on the results 
of these scans, the exact test matrix can be modified as necessary for further runs.

Due to the large number of conditions to be tested and the limited amount of gases

involves the stabilization time necessary to change between different flow conditions, 
specifically when changing the ratio of fuel to inert. To minimize this time, the

velocity has been observed to produce a steady flame within seconds. This 
improvement allows for data acquisition on the next test condition to begin without

carried out at the different fluid veloc ities until extinction is detected. Once the 
extinction limit is reached for a particular dilution level, the flow conditions will be 
reset to a healthy ignition setting and reignited.
