text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 4 
2.5 The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT 
The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a 
microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI. The P-Trak is a 
hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 
microns. 
After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the P-
Trak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, 
resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment. 
P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time while storing that data in a memory maintained by an on-
board battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol 
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the 
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter). These droplets have many times the average 
diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques. The potential 
problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a 
predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ 
down hill. 
In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, 
effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics. Furthermore, 
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be 
counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. 
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were 
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which 
the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, 
inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit. 
The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible 
to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the 
duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance). This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of 
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment.

Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified

To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail

4.0 SAME CREW INTERFACES 
4.1 Hardware Subsystem Description 
The major planned components of SAME are as follows. They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which 
they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 
1. Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) 
The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled 
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including 
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG 
fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids 
resources accordingly. Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, 
and the other fluids system functions. 
2. Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 
This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate 
which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it 
are: 
• The Smoke Generation Tube 
• The Video Camera and Controller 
• The Sample Positioning system including: 
o the Sample Turning Module 
o the sample engagement mechanism 
o the sample position indicator 
o the sample positioning lock mechanism 
o the Sample Carousel mounting system

file: documents/PSI-101/PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 6 
3. Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) 
The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: 
the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial 
Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low 
internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the 
requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as 
controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the 
VES for exhaust and purging. 
4. Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) 
The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated 
Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and 
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal 
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow 
accordingly. Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains 
a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 
5. Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) 
The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of 
the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the 
Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for 
subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record 
of the pyrolysis event. 
6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) 
The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the 
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the 
Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate 
independently and store its own data. 
7. Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) 
The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. 
Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The 
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot. 
8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180)

file: documents/PSI-101/PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
d for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The 
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot. 
8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) 
The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its 
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure 
the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to 
increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by 
software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 
9. Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) 
The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. 
It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the 
DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 7 
10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) 
The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke 
Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially 
installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify 
the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which 
allows the sample to be in a position to be energized. The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: 
Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small 
section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless 
steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its 
varying resistance). 
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and 
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) 
The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope 
(TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS. The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the 
carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 
12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) 
The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick 
required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally 
required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 
13. Hoses 
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to 
power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are 
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic 
hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not 
typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 
14. Harnessing 
All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make 
the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability.

This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements.

Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in 
smoke evolution.

4.2 Video Recording Devices 
Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in 
smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always 
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is 
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on 
and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 
4.3 On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions 
The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, 
Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and 
disassemble the experiment.

5.0 SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 
5.1 Software Controlled Operational Functions 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing 
with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as 
well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG. The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke 
system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground. The software can autonomously control the progress of 
preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG 
video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink. The software inside the DACU is 
also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 
5.2 Data Collection 
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information. The Thermal Precipitator Module, 
which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis. Sample Carousels are retained so that the 
samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 
6.0 SAME OPERATIONS 
6.1 Operations Flow 
1. Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of 
the MSG. Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components. After 
the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed 
onto the MSG Laptop. 
2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load 
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module. Next, the 
start-up check out routine is performed. After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated. Then, 
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again 
until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used. The next number matched Sample Carousel and 
Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 
3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments 
have been performed, the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged. 
In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing. 
6.2 Detailed Operations 
Please refer to the SAME Operations Concept Document (SAME-DOC-009) for a more detailed description of all 
Operations functions.

7.0 SAFETY CONCERNS & PREVENTATIVE MEASURES 
7.1 Overall Strategy 
Safety analysis is being performed for the SAME (formerly Smoke) hardware in accordance with the safety policies and 
safety requirements for flight hardware (NSTS1700.7B and ISS Addendum). This assessment is being prepared using 
NSTS 13830C as a guideline for data submittal. Hazards not eliminated by design are addressed in either the latest revision 
of standardized hazard control report JSC Form 1230 for ISS and launch/landing phase of the mission or in a Unique 
Hazard Report, JSC 542B. For the most part, the SAME experiment uses generic hazard controls for electrical power 
hazards, sharp edges, EMI (testing), rotating equipment (smaller than 8 inch diameter rotors and less than 8000 RPM), Fire 
Detection and suppression, and touch temperature. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

7.2 Pressurized Systems 
The pressure system includes the aging chamber, the system for moving the piston in the aging chamber (valves, regulator, 
lines, hoses, relief devices) and the Dynamic Diluter. All of the parts will be designed to meet the requirements of 
NSTS1700.7 ISS addendum, NASA-STD-5003, SSP 30558, and SSP 52005 for pressurized hardware. Pressurized lines 
and fittings will be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 200 psid (ISS N2 limiting pressure). Pressurized 
system components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP of 200 psid. Down 
stream of the pressure reduction the MDP is 20 psig. These components are designed with the same factors of safety. See 
table of components and factors of safety and hazard report SMOKE-04. Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress 
corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and 
Processes. In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will 
not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001) specifically hazard report 
SMOKE-04. 
7.3 Structures 
The SAME experiment is launched in stowage and contained in MSG for on orbit use. The structural aspect of SAME is 
primarily sealed containers and vented containers. Pressure systems are covered in section 1.2. SAME structural failure is 
addressed in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
7.4 Materials 
The ZIN Tech Engineering Team will assure that reasonable measures have been taken with regard to material selection for 
the experiment‘s design, and selected materials are safe for the intended manned space flight application in their respective 
usage environment. A material flammability assessment will be performed per NSTS 22648. The flight unit will be offgas 
tested. The SAME Project Team will prepare the standard Materials Identification & Usage List (MIUL) and MUA’s. ZIN 
Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to 
NASA/GRC/SMAD for concurrence. Upon material evaluation approval, NASA/GRC/SMTD will issue the Material 
Certification Letter in accordance with the guidelines established in the applicable Material and Processes (M&P) 
Intercenter Agreement prior to flight hardware fabrication. Further information can be found in Hazard Report SMOKE 
STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
7.5 Frangible Materials (Glass) 
All of the hardware which contains glass will undergo a vibration test in the stowed configuration at workmanship or 
protoflight levels and a post-test visual inspection to verify ability to survive launch loads. The duct with the video camera 
lens and LEDs installed will be stowed with clear plastic for crew inspection after launch.

7.6 Release of Experiment By-products into the Cabin Atmosphere 
The P-Trak needs a cartridge with an alcohol-saturated wick for its operation; therefore, a risk of contaminating the ISS 
environment has to be considered. The amount of alcohol released will be carefully controlled and limited. The Project 
Team will submit a Volatile Usage Agreement request to JSC/OC (Material and Processes) for disposition and approval. 
All payloads are to submit their usage requests to a single approval authority at JSC because alcohol usage is a cumulative 
risk, and it will be necessary to process VUA through a single approval authority to track the total quantity of alcohol being 
used. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SMOKE-SDP-001). 
The pyrolysis products of Teflon currently have a JSC Tox level 3 for 5 minutes after creation. After this point the particles 
coalesce and drop to tox level 0. A hazard report has been generated to address this issue. The smoke is contained in the 
smoke tube and aging chamber for 5 minutes. All the smoke is expelled through HEPA filters, some of which dumps into 
the ISS vent the rest of it into the MSG. The MSG is the second containment of the smoke if the aging chamber where to 
leak. Finally the MSG is under a negative pressure which would prevent the smoke from leaking in the event of an MSG 
leak. Hazard Report SAME-08 has been written and submitted to the PSRP for review.

7.7 Non-Ionizing Laser Radiation 
The ISS Smoke Detector, the P-Trak and the DustTrak contain lasers as a part of their diagnostics systems. These lasers are 
of Class 1 lasers, and the laser beams are fully contained. These items are not removed from their original housings and are 
used in the applications for which they are intended. There is no crew access to the lasers at any time. The lasers meet 
ANSI Z136.1-2000 standards for Class 1. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

The STS Smoke detector and the First Alert Smoke Alarm each contain 1 micro curie of Americium-241. These items are 
not removed from their original housings and are used in the applications for which they are intended. More detail can be 
found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

In order to assure the overall quality and performance of the systems created by the project team, Product Assurance will be 
provided by the ZIN Quality team and will include but not be limited to oversight of the manufacturing and assembly 
processes, investigations into materials and their compatibilities, compliance with the Safety requirements, assessment of 
the systems controls (i.e. Software) and inspection of the final products. The specific methods and strategies planned can be 
found in the following documents: SAME Product Assurance Plan (SAME-PLN-003) and Same Software Assurance Plan 
(SAME-PLN-006). Please refer to them for more detail.

2.0 IN-FLIGHT FUNCTIONAL CHECKLIST 
This is a list of items that should be addressed after the hardware is installed in the MSG and before any 
samples are tested. Not currently in any order. 
- Perform piston calibration and alter registry values as necessary. See procedure later in this 
document. Run a test with heater setpoint below R0 and no use of the thermal precipitors in order 
to confirm correct calibration. 
- Figure out good values for STSPumpFailureLowLimit and STSPumpFailureHighLimit registry 
values. These depend somewhat on atmospheric pressure and should be adjusted for the ISS 
environment. Correctly set, these values help detect failure of the STS pump. 
- Log some data with the P-Trak and DustTrak and confirm that their settings are correct. For 
example: log interval, time constant, and date/time. 
- Record some video, downlink, and examine. 
- Experimentally determine the maximum setpoints that the mass flow controller will meet given 
ISS vacuum and GN2 sources. Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic 
combinations are affected. 
- The registry value, DisableChecksumCheck, can be set to 1 to avoid the startup delay associated 
with calculating the checksum each time. 
- Revisit the decision about whether the heater controller offset correction will be done 
automatically as part of the test sequence or manually using the HeaterCorrectOffset utility prior 
to the test sequence. Adjust the CorrectOffset registry value appropriately.

3.0 STARTING THE SOFTWARE 
3.1 Ground Computer 
On the ground computer you’ll need to first log on. Then start TReK with SAME configuration files. 
Also start SAMEDisplay. More TBD. 
3.2 SAME Flight Software 
The software that controls the system starts automa tically upon power on. Within 30 seconds of turning 
on 120V power to the system there should be telemetr y data received at the SAMEDisplay application. 
The GMT will be updating and startup messages will appear in the log window. The Run Mode will 
change from Startup to Unitialized.

4.0 TEST CHECKLIST 
This is a list of important things to do or confirm pr ior to, during, and after the running of a sample test. 
Placement of a highly visible printout of this lis t on console is recommended. Steps depend on whether 
sample heater offset correction is being done automatically or manually. Check the CorrectOffset registry 
value to find out (0=manual, >0=automatic). 
- Once per carousel open the gate valves and turn on the diagnostics for TBD minutes. Downlink 
the data and verify correctness. The purpose is to collect baseline measurements of the MSG work 
volume required by the science team. 
4.1 With Automatic Heater Offset Correction 
- Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. 
- Send the Initialize command. 
- If the desired sample is not engaged, engage it using the Self Test command. 
- Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. 
- Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance. If they differ 
significantly, TBD. Determine the setpoint. 
- Look at test parameters and change as necessary. Use manual positioning option, but carousel and 
sample number must be correct. 
- Start the test. 
- When the test pauses check the following: 
o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. 
o The offset correction returned a value less than 50uV in the log. 
o The sample resistance is still good. Within TBD % of before. 
o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. 
o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good. Range is TBD. 
- If the offset correction returned a value greater than 50uV, abort the test and restart. If the offset is 
still greater than 50uV, change the CorrectOffset registry value to 0 (manual) and use the manual 
heater offset correction checklist instead. 
- Resume the test. 
- Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start. When it does, be ready to send 
an Abort command. 
- Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt. The software will 
too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send 
the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. 
- After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. 
- After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest 
logged test ids. Turn back off. 
- As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC. Their transfer 
during power down has a slight chance of failing. Doing it here ensures success. 
- Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. 
- Disengage the sample. 
- Send the Shutdown command with Shutdown option and power off system, or proceed to next 
test.

Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that

environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware 
condition, perhaps after many tests have been run. 
7.3.1 Inlet Velocity 
Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inle t velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec. Actual velocity 
is not a directly measured value. It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and

7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time 
Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston 
reaches the top of the chamber. Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at 
the end of heating enters the chamber as well. And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows 
the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber. The amount of the latter clean air is 
determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value. 
Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the 
software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take. Then it can back off 
from there to determine sample heating stop and start times. The registry values, FillWaita.b, where a.b is 
0.0 to 5.0 by 0.5, help compensate for timing inconsis tencies which are a function of fill rate in LPM. 
(These values were more drastically a function of f ill rate before the FillLeakRateLPM registry value was 
increased from 0.0. See section 7.3.1.). 
Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM 
until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia. These values have been determined to be reliable, but can 
be changed if necessary by altering the registry values, FillStartRateLPM and FillStartPressurePSIA. 
Then the software waits for a period determined by th e desired fill rate, a function of inlet velocity, and 
the FillWait registry values. For a fill rate of 3.0 the software waits for the value of FillWait3.0. For rates 
in between, the wait time is interpolated. After wai ting this time the software marks the start of piston 
movement, logging a message for the user. Sample heating and other start and stop times are based on

7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume 
When a secondary aging period and volume are speci fied, the piston must stop a percentage of the 
distance between the top and bottom of the chamber. There is no direct physical measurement of the 
running distance, therefore it is estimated from th e exhaust rate over time. The registry value, 
ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage. To adjust this value, 
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage. For best results use the 
exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test. Or use 5 LPM and 
50%. 
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way. Use the same rate and 100%. 
- Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the 
percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust. Adjust the registry value and repeat until 
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage. 
7.3.4 Exhaust Rate 
It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct 
for all combinations of diagnostic use except when usi ng the STS detector with both DustTraks. If this 
situation changes, the exhaust rate can be increased using the ExhaustOverpressureRate registry value.

7.5 Description of HeaterCorrectOffset Utility 
Sample heater offset correction is a feature of the sample heater microcontroller that reduces 
measurement error by automatically removing off set voltages from the signal path. After offset 
correction is performed, all subsequent resistance me asurements will include the o ffset correction. Until 
the system is powered off, that is. At power up the offset correction is zero. Offset correction should be 
run for each sample while the sample is engaged with the inlet tube and sample heater contacts. 
Occasionally the offset correction circuitry produces a co rrection that is obviously too high. The result is 
that subsequent reports of resistance are lower than ac tual. This can be detected at the time of the test 
pause by looking at the sample resistance and by lo oking for the log message indicating the value of the 
offset correction. It should be approximately 200uV or less. 
If the offset correction at the time of the test pause is too high, then the test must be aborted and restarted 
to give the offset correction circuitry a second chan ce. To avoid this time-consuming detour a utility 
separate from the flight software has been developed. It is HeaterCorrectOffset_g in the /root directory of 
the DACU. It can be run from the flight software by sending the OSCommand command with a 
parameter of ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. 
The HeaterCorrectOffset utility app lies 12VDC to the sample heater , waits a few seconds, and then 
requests an offset correction from the heater microcontro ller. If the returned off set is in range then the 
utility exits, otherwise it requests the offset correction ag ain for several times until it is in range. Either 
way, 12VDC is removed from the sample heater befo re the utility exists. As long as system power (not 
12VDC) remains applied, the offset correction initiated by the utility will be used by the flight software. 
If the utility fails to correct the offset to within the desired range then it returns a -1 (which is reported in 
the flight software log as 65280), otherwise it returns a zero to indicate success. 
There is one caveat to running the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. The flight software must be either not 
running, which will not occur during flight, or must be in the uninitialized state. Once the software is

lity fails to correct the offset to within the desired range then it returns a -1 (which is reported in 
the flight software log as 65280), otherwise it returns a zero to indicate success. 
There is one caveat to running the HeaterCorrectOffset utility. The flight software must be either not 
running, which will not occur during flight, or must be in the uninitialized state. Once the software is 
initialized the utility cannot gain serial access to the heater micr ocontroller. Thus the sequence 
gymnastics in section 4.0. 
Additionally, if the HeaterCorrectOffset utility is used, then offset correction prior to the test pause should 
be disabled. Otherwise an incorrect correction he re will negate the use of the utility. Setting the 
CorrectOffset registry value to zero will disable au tomatic offset correction during the test, allowing the 
value created by the HeaterCorrectOffset utility to be used.

8.0 KNOWN ISSUES 
- Aborting a test occasionally causes the software to restart. If this should happen you’ll need to 
reissue the Initialize command. 
- Try to avoid running a test sequence through the change of hour (i.e. 12:45-13:05). Transfer of 
the housekeeping file at the top of the hour takes a good bit of processor time and the processor is 
close to 100% capacity, possibly affecting diagnostic measurement retrieval. 
- It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the 
System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. However, about 20% of the time the software 
will hang or restart before completely shutting down. If it restarts, issue the Shutdown command 
again or issue the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. If it hangs (you may only 
know this if you have a monitor connected to the GSE port) a hard power off will have to suffice. 
The operating system will clean up any file ‘litter’ on the next power up. 
- Maximum inlet velocity with the FillLeakRateLPM registry value equal to 0.30 is 9.8 cm/sec. 
Above this the software does not correctly use the FillWait registry values to time chamber fill 
operations, including sample heating start time. 10.0 cm/sec can be achieved if FillLeakRateLPM 
is 0.25 LPM or less. But timing is affected in other ways and ground testing or flight testing 
without sample heating is recommended. 
- Whenever the P-Trak is on, the DACU requests a measurement from it once per second. 
Occasionally the P-Trak does not respond with a measurement and the DACU substitutes a -999 
value instead to mark this occurance. If the P-Trak is logging during this time, that missing data 
can be recovered by issuing the Transfer Data command to retrieve the logged data. It is 
recommended that this be done for each test, soon (within days) after the test is complete. 
- The P-Trak memory can hold approximately 60 20-minute tests. When all memory is used the 
unit does not respond with any serial measurements while logging. In other words, continuous -
999 readings is one indicator of full memory. It is suggested that memory be cleared after 50 
tests to be safe. 
- Sample heater offset correction occasionally produces an incorrect correction factor. The result is 
that reported sample resistance is lower than actual. For more information see section 7.5. 
- Using ground support equipment there was insufficient fluid flow during chamber exhaust to 
maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct, as required, when the STS detector and both 
DustTraks are in use. When the STS detector is used it is recommended that at most one 
DustTrak is used. 
- If the heater gives an “Abort on MaxRt” error, the system must be power cycled before 
proceeding. Otherwise, as will be apparent, the resistance measurement will be in error. 
- When specifying inlet velocities below 2 cm/sec, the FillWait registry values may not be 
accurate.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) 
 
 
Abstract 
 
Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the 
design of the environmental control and life-su pport system on spacecraft. While prevention is 
certainly the first line of defens e against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual 
fire allows the crew to res pond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options 
available for response to a spacecraft fire increas e the importance of dete cting the fire in an 
earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. This report describes 
the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment 
conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) 
to characterize the size distribution of smoke part iculate produced in low- gravity from a variety 
of overheated spacecraft material s The absence of gravity can im pact not only the formation of 
the smoke particulate but also th e aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate 
are transported from their source to a detector. 
 
Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in th e Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, 
(Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles gene rated and observed in low gravity 
environment tend to be larger in size than t hose in earth conditions. Ho wever, the preliminary 
results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot 
wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could 
not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. 
Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle 
size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment was designed to obtain this data 
that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration 
missions. Unfortunately, because of the relati vely small volume of the MSG, it cannot 
accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size 
distribution of smoke particul ate. Therefore, a new proce dure was developed, the moment 
method, from which the characteristics of the part icle size distribution can be inferred using a 
minimum number of portable instrument. 
 
The SAME experiments were conducted during E xpedition 15 on the ISS. Four materials, 
typical of those found in spacecr aft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, 
silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fift h material, dibutyl-phthalate (D BP) retained in a cotton wick 
was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, 
samples were heated to temperatures below th e ignition point. The smoke generation conditions

typical of those found in spacecr aft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, 
silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fift h material, dibutyl-phthalate (D BP) retained in a cotton wick 
was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, 
samples were heated to temperatures below th e ignition point. The smoke generation conditions 
were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The 
transport time from the smoke source to the det ector was simulated by holding the smoke in an 
aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds. Smoke particle samples 
were collected on Transmission Electron Microsc ope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The 
smoke properties were measured using particulat e aerosol diagnostics that measure different 
moments of the size distribution. These statistic s were combined to determine the geometric 
mean particle sizes and geometric standard devia tion, which is sufficient to describe the entire 
smoke distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. For comparison, smoke detectors from

the ISS and the space shuttle we re also included in the SAME apparatus. The experimental 
results show that, for the materials tested, a su bstantial portion of the smoke particles are below 
500 nm in diameter. The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke 
transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The 
knowledge gained from SAME can be used to es tablish design requirements for smoke detectors 
used in future spacecraft.

1. Introduction 
 
Appropriate design of fire detection systems require s knowledge of both the expected signature of the 
events to be detected and the bac kground levels of the measured parame ters. Terrestrial fire detection 
systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires. 1, 2 Unfortunately, there is no 
corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and cons equently current spacecraft fire detectors were 
developed based upon experience on normal gravity fi re behavior and propertie s. This approach was 
necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned 
spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will requi re increased reliability of fire 
detection systems in addition to robust false alar m resistance. Extended lunar-surface missions will 
require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources. 
The absence of buoyant flow increas es the residence time in microgra vity fires causing substantial 
changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire beha vior seen in reduced gravity, it is 
reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are 
a number of factors that can be expected to aff ect the particle size distri bution of the smoke from 
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in 
microgravity fires and increases the transit ti me from the reaction zone to the detector. 3 The materials 
used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke 
properties were previously evaluate d. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a 
spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is 
typical for terrestrial applications. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size 
distribution. The objective of this work was to ma ke sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft 
fires to enable improved design of future detectors. 
2. Smoke Background 
 
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In 
particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol incl udes recondensed original material or pyrolysis 
products that can be either liquid or solid. For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, 
condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot part icles dominate the smoke pa rticulate in established 
flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer frag ments are produced by 
smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fi re growth. Given the constrained space on any 
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established 
flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.

the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The S kylab module, however, included approximately 30 
UV-sensing fire detectors. 4 These devices were limited to line-of -sight and were reported to have 
difficulties with false alarms. 
 
Details of the ISS and STS detector require ments are described by Steisslinger et al. 6 A brief overview 
of the requirements is given below.

The STS measurements included the results from two cascade impactors and a light scattering device. 
The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 
2.5 μm to 10 μm and >100 μm ranges. The other two ranges <2.5 μm and 10 μm to 100 μm were very 
lightly populated. Each impact or sampled approximately 15 m 3 of air over approximately 30 hours. 
These results showed substantially higher concentr ations than typical indoor measurements (over a 
factor of 5 for the two most populat ed size ranges). These data were supported by the li ght scattering 
instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 loca tions, all of these reported mass concentrations 
ranging from 50 μg/m3 to 70 μg/m3. The ISS results of Urban et al. 5 were obtained from a feasibility 
experiment to validate the operation of an aerosol particle counter in low-gravity (DAFT). The 
measurements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise 
level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm 3). The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the 
STS and the low overall numbers for the ISS suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection 
since typical normal gravity fires produce su bstantial particulate in this size range 5,2 However more 
complete particle size statistics are needed. 
 
3. SAME Experiment 
 
To address the limited data from the CSD experime nt concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke 
particulate, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement E xperiment (SAME) was developed. The SAME 
experiment sought to avoid the problems experi enced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the 
particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a 
challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typica lly too large to be compatible 
with spacecraft experiment constraints. Thus, to obtai n particulate size statistics with existing aerosol 
instrumentation would require the return of numerous samples to Earth. As will be described below, an 
alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of 
the size distribution. When combine d, these moments provide useful a ggregate statistics of the size 
distribution if a lognormal distri bution is assumed. The measurem ents were made using smoke 
generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however 
the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.

A. The Moment Method 
 
The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience. 13 This 
approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (the zeroth, first and third moment) 
on orbit, using several small, light -weight instruments. By applyi ng the properties of the lognormal 
distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, Nt, the geometric mean diameter, 
Dg, and the geometric standard deviation, g, of the aerosol can be estimated. Once these three 
parameters are known, the size distribution of the m easured aerosol is uniquely defined, assuming that 
the distribution is lognormal. In what follows, we will explain how the moment method works.

distribution function can be expre ssed as a frequency (or density) di stribution function or a cumulative 
distribution function. Then, each of the two can be expressed in terms of its normalized form or non-

A.2. Implementation of the moment method in SAME experiment 
 
In the SAME experiment, the zeroth moment, M0, was measured using a c ondensation nuclei counter 
called the P-Trak TM (TSI Inc.). The first moment, M1, was approximately pr oportional to the output 
signal of an ionization detector, which was a modified ionization chamber taken from a commercially-
available smoke detector. The third moment, M3, was inferred from the li ght scattered by the smoke 
aerosol when illuminated by a red laser. For particles in th e size range of 0.2 μm to 2.0 μm, , the light 
scattering signal at 90 degrees from a red laser is approximately proportional to the third moment. The 
instrument used to obtain the third moment is called a DustTrakTM (TSI Inc.). Calibration measurements 
were made for the DustTrak to account for th e departure of the scattering signal from the 3 rd moment. 
More detailed information of instruments and thei r operations can be found in the Instruments section 
below. The instruments used in SAME were compact enough to be installed in the ISS MSG. 
 
Extensive calibrations of these instruments were performed at NIST to ensure that correct values of each 
moment were obtained from the instrument output sign als. The results of these calibrations showed that 
the instrument signals correlate well with corresponding moments ex cept for the third moment. The 
third moment was found to be a function of the DustTr ak output and the particle diameters. This led to 
an iterative procedure to find the best-fit results of Dg and g.

B. Instrumentation 
 
The moment measurements were made using an a ssembly of three separate instruments. Two are 
industrial hygiene instruments manufactured by TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector. 
 
The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei counter, the P- Trak™ (TSI Inc.). This device 
operates by passing the aerosol-laden air stream through a region satura ted with isopropanol vapor and 
then into a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particles increasing their diameter such that 
they can be readily counted by a light scattering devi ce. This instrument is very robust and operates 
over a range of 0 to 10 5 particles/cm3 and 20 nm to 1 μm diameter. Some diluti on is required since the 
smoke concentration in SAME ranges from about 0.5 × 10 6 to 5 × 10 6 particles/cm3. There was also a 
concern that the isopropanol condensate woul d not return to the wick in low-gravity. 5 To mitigate this

10 
 
issue, the condensing section of the device was modified with very small grooves to improve 
conductance of the condensate back to the wick. These changes were tested in a separate space 
experiment with good results indicating the modified device could be used successfully in low gravity.5 
 
The first-moment instrument is the ionization cham ber taken from a resident ial smoke detector. This 
device uses an alpha-particle emitter to generate ions in a region within a DC electric field. Normally, 
the ions drift toward an electrode inside the ioni zation chamber producing a current. When particulate 
are present, the ions attach themselves to the pa rticles thereby charging the particles. Because the 
charged particles have a much smaller mobility than ions alone, the current is reduced. The required 
particle concentrations are on the order of 105 particles/cm3, thus no sample dilution was required. 
 
The third-moment instrument is a light scattering de vice, the DustTrak™ (TSI In c.). The device uses a 
90 degree light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass density. For terrestrial dust particulate, this 
signal correlates well with the mass concentration, however additional comp ensation was needed to 
account for the range of particle sizes observed in the SAME experiment. The device operating range is 
from 0.001 mg/m3 to 100 mg /m3. These devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at the inlet 
which captures particles larger than the selected size. The SAME experiment included 2 DustTraks™, 
one with a 1 μm impactor and the other with a 10 μm impactor. The differen ce in the signal from the 
two devices provided a measure of the fraction of the particulate that was larger than 1 μm. In some 
cases dilution was required owing to the high smoke concentration levels.

video and uplink commanding. Smoke was generated by resistively heating small samples of spacecraft 
materials. Sample heating wa s achieved by heating a steel wire that was wrapped around an 
approximately 3 mm diameter cylinder of the sample material. The steel wire was resistively heated and

C. Instrument Calibration 
 
Calibration of these instruments was essential to prope rly interpret the flight data and was performed on 
the ground before the flight. Calibra tion was accomplished using two different aerosol generators; one 
generates mono-disperse particle using dioctyl phthalate (DOP) according to the approach by 
Mulholland and Liu 19 and the other uses polysty rene spheres. The monodi sperse droplet generator 
functioned by producing a spray of DOP diluted with isopropanol wh ich is then evaporated and 
recondensed producing monodisperse droplets. The droplet size is controlled by the DOP dilution level. 
The generator will operate stably for tens of minutes. The aerosol from the generator was sampled 
simultaneously by the SAME instru ment under test and a reference instrument. For the number count, 
the reference instrument was a TSI 3022 particle count er, for the mass concentration of the aerosol, a 
Tapered Element Oscillating Microbalance and for th e first moment a TSI Elect rical Aerosol Detector 
was used. The results for the P-Trak are shown in Fi g. 7. As the number c oncentration increases, the 
effect of the particle diameter becomes more evid ent. Separate correlations were developed for each 
particle size and the closes t correlation was used to analyze the flight data based on the initial estimates 
of the average particle size.

4. Flight Tests 
 
The SAME hardware installed in the ISS MSG is s hown in Fig 10. The SAME tests were performed on 
board ISS in September and early October of 2007. Overall 30 sample materials were tested. These 
were comprised of six samples each of 5 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, silicone rubber, cellulose, and 
dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a por ous wick. These samples were test ed at different airflow rates, 
pyrolysis temperatures, and smoke aging durations. 
 
Realizing that crew time was the most precious I SS resource, SAME was desi gned to be operated both 
autonomously and from the ground to the greatest exte nt possible. The SAME hardware was organized 
into a number of smaller modular un its to facilitate stow age for launch, provide for easy change out, 
increase the reliability a nd reduce risk. The downside of this st rategy was that the assembly of the 
experiment involved many connections and required approximately 5 hours of crew time. Once installed, 
however, SAME was easily and effectively operated fr om the Tele Science Center (TSC) at the Glenn 
Research Center (GRC), and this ca pability enabled the ground team to achieve roughl y a 50% greater 
number of test points (and data) than was originally planned. 
The on orbit operations were scheduled around the availability of the crew for installing the next Sample 
Carousel and Thermal Precipitator (and removing and stowing the used ones). Typically, the crew would 
install the next units during the morning, and operati ons would be scheduled for later that day. SAME 
would be nominally scheduled by the ISS staff for two test points on each of the following days. 
 
Figure 10. SAME Experiment installed in the ISS MSG Facility.

15 
 
Because the allowed operations windows were sufficiently large, the ground team was frequently able to 
perform four test points in the allowed time. 
The staffing level of the ground team varied between two and five me mbers from the engineering team 
with additional support from up to three members of the Science team. Most of the time, there would be 
one person operating the linked co mputer that controlled the expe riment, one providing verbal 
communication to the ISS cadre an d doing data reduction and a third recording video and performing 
other miscellaneous functions. 
Uplink parameter sheets were generated by the Science team and most times, emailed to the engineering 
team the day before operations, although when additional unplanned test points were performed during a 
session, the Science team provided a hard copy of the parameters during the interim between test points. 
These sheets were printed and checked, and in most cas es, signed. The parameters were entered into the 
ground computer by a team member and then the en try was checked both by means of a checksum and 
by the other member on consol before uplinking them to the DACU. 
The test points were scheduled by the ground team to coincide with Ku and S band coverage so that 
video of the heating and the measurement data coul d be obtained Near Real Time (NRT) and recorded 
on the ground. Because the data reduction software was already in place, processing of the data could be 
done immediately after the test point had been completed, and in all cases, before the next test point was 
performed. Periodically during the overall operations, downloads from the DACU were commanded as a 
backup to the NRT data to insure that the most complete compilation was available. 
Detailed chronological record of the SAME flight tests can be found in Appendix A.

In general, since the mass increases with the cube of the diameter, the larger particles do not affect the 
count mean diameter (CMD) as much as they affect the light scattering signa l which scales with the 
particle mass. Consequently, although the CMD for silicone rubber is 189 nm, almost half the particle 
mass is larger than 1 m, as evidenced by the ratio of the Dust Trak instruments. The lamp wick shows 
similar behavior. 
On the other hand, the Kapton and Teflon show substan tially narrower particle size distributions with 
little mass in particles larger than 1m. These low populations of larger particles are consistent with the 
less effective detection by light scat tering devices which was seen for so me of the Teflon tests and with 
the signals obtained from the STS a nd ISS detectors. All of the tests conducted in this series of 
experiments show strong signals on the Space Shuttle detector (ionization) despite the larger particle 
size distributions seen for the lamp wick (cellulose) and silicone rubber. The CSD experiment5 reported 
poor detection by the Space Shuttle detector for non- flaming overheat of cellulose and silicone rubber 
(indicating larger particle sizes). The reduced signal on the Space Shuttle detector for CSD suggests that 
under some reasonable pre-fire conditions the smoke size distribution can extend to diameters beyond 
those seen in the SAME experiment. 
The TEM grids recovered from the thermal precipi tators were unfortunately contaminated with 
extraneous particles whose origin was believed to be somewhere in the assembly of the thermal

6. Closing Remarks 
 
The SAME project successf ully implemented the moment method de scribed in this report, under the 
volume constraints of the ISS MSG, to determine th e size distribution of th e smokes generated from 5 
tested materials in well controlled conditions of heat ing temperature, heating tim e and air flow rate. In 
combination with the knowledge gained from prev ious CSD experiment, it becomes obvious that the 
detection of smoke across the size range seen in SA ME and CSD, while still discriminating against dust 
(which tends to be large), will prob ably require a detection system that can discriminate the particle size 
distribution to at least a limited degree. Two possible effective means of achieving this size 
discrimination are to employ a detector that measures more than one mo ment of the size distribution or 
to use a detector that can classify the particles into size ranges.

ABSTRACT 
This paper presents results from a smoke detection 
experiment entitled Smoke Aerosol Measurement 
Experiment (SAME) which was conducted in the 
Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International 
Space Station (ISS) during Expedition 15. Five different 
materials representative of those found in spacecraft 
were pyrolyzed at temperatures below the ignition point 
with conditions controlled to provide repeatable sample 
surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The 
sample materials were Teflon®, Kapton®, cellulose, 
silicone rubber and dibutylphthalate. The transport time 
from the smoke source to the detector was simulated by 
holding the smoke in an aging chamber for times 
ranging from 10 to1800 seconds. Smoke particle 
samples were collected on Transmission Electron 
Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The 
smoke particle size distributions were measured using 
three particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure 
different moments of the size distribution and smoke 
detectors from the ISS and the space shuttle. These 
diagnostics were used to estimate the particle number 
concentration (zeroth moment), the diameter 
concentration (first moment) and the mass concentration 
(third moment). These values were combined to 
estimate the diameter of average mass, the count mean 
diameter, the geometric mean diameter and the 
geometric standard deviation. Even though the analysis 
of these data is ongoing, information from the various 
instruments and the calculated mean particle sizes has 
important implications for the design of spacecraft 
smoke detectors. These implications are reviewed in this

INTRODUCTION 
Design of fire detector systems requires understanding 
of the background conditions and the expected range of 
events to be detected. Dete ctors for terrestrial fires 
were developed using the result s of extensive study of 
terrestrial fires. 1,2 Unfortunately, there is no 
corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and 
consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were 
developed based upon experience from terrestrial 
systems. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen 
in reduced gravity, it is reasonable to expect that the 
smoke characteristics and detection requirements of 
these fires will change. The absence of buoyant flow in

SMOKE BACKGROUND 
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol 
materials produced by a number of processes. In 
particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original 
polymer or pyrolysis products that can be liquid, solid, 
carbonaceous soot, condensed water vapor, or ash 
particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate 
in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis 
products and recondensed polymer fragments are 
produced by smoldering and pyro lysis in the early stage 
of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any 
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is 
necessarily the early phase and not established flaming 
fires; consequently, the primar y target for detection is 
the pyrolysis products and not the soot. 
Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more detail 
in papers by Friedman and Urban. 4,5 In the Mercury, 
Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were 
limited and mission durations were short. Consequently 
it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would 
rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, 
included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors. 4 
These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were 
reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The 
Space Shuttle (Space Trans portation System (STS)) 
detectors were based upon ionization fire detector 
technology, the most advanced technology available at 
the time and used an inertial separator designed to 
eliminate particles larger than 1-2 micrometers. The 
International Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use 
near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most 
sensitive to particles larger than a micrometer, outside of 
the range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector. 
More details of the ISS and STS detector requirements 
are presented by Steisslinger et al. 6 however the basic 
details are summarized below. The STS detector, as 
built, was designed to alarm at 2 mg/m 3 (based on 1 
micrometer particles) or 0.022 mg/m 3/s rise in 
concentration for 20 seconds. The ISS detector was 
designed to alarm at obscuration of 1% per foot using an 
Underwriters Laboratory (UL) smoke box and a white

 As described by Friedman 4 there have been six 
overheat and failed component failures in the NASA 
Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents that 
have occurred on the ISS. None of these events spread 
into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the 
likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 
1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation 
systems can have significant consequences. As a result, 
improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is 
critically needed.7 
Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity 
sources by Urban et al .5 found that the particulate 
produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel 
particles) tends to have larger size particles than in 
normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative 
Soot Diagnostics) Experiment 5 which studied smoke 
properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft 
materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could 
achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate 
remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the 
CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data 
concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide 
detector design. The combined impact of these limited 
results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to 
extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g 
combustion particulate is needed for more confident 
design of smoke detectors for spacecraft.

INSTRUMENTS 
More details of the experiment hardware and its 
calibration are presented elsewhere,11,12 however a brief 
summary follows. The moment measurements were 
made using an assembly of th ree separate instruments. 
Two are industrial hygiene instruments manufactured by 
TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector. 
The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei 
counter P-Trak® (TSI Inc.). This device operates by 
passing the aerosol-laden particle stream through a 
region saturated with isopropanol vapor and then into a 
cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the 
particles increasing their diam eter such that they can be 
readily counted by a light scattering detector. This 
instrument is very robust and operates over a range of 0 
to 10 5 particles/cm 3 and 20 nm to 4 to 5 μm diameter. 
Some dilution is required, since the allowable smoke 
concentration ranges from about 0.5 × 10 6 to 5 × 10 6 
particles / cm3. 
The first-moment instrument is an ionization chamber 
from a residential smoke detector. This device uses an 
alpha-particle emitter (Am 241) to generate ions in a 
region within a DC electric field. The drift of the ions in 
the electric field results in a current. The presence of 
particulate reduces the current as a result of the 
attachment of the ions to the particulate. The mobility of 
the charged aerosol is too small for it to be collected on 
the ionization chamber electrode. The required particle 
concentrations are on the order of 105 particles/cm3, and 
no sample dilution was required. 
The third-moment instrument is a light scattering device 
DustTrak® (TSI Inc.). The device measures the 
intensity of light scattered by the smoke aerosol at a 
scattering angle of about 90 degrees light scattering 
signal to quantify the aerosol mass. This light scattering 
signal is approximately proportional to the mass 
concentration; however, to compensate for the non-
linearity of the relationship between mass and the 
scattering signal density, additional analysis based on 
Mie Scattering theory or calibration with the specific 
aerosol material is required. The device’s operating 
range is from 0.001 mg/m 3 to 100 mg/m 3. These 
devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at 
the inlet which captures particles larger than the 
selected size. The SAME experiment included 2 
DustTraks® one with a 1 μm impactor and one with a 10 
μm impactor. The difference in the signal from these 
two devices provided a measur e of the fraction of the 
particulate that was larger than 1 μm. In some cases 
dilution was required owing to the high smoke 
concentration levels.

2. The system was install ed in the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox, an ISS facility that provides many resources 
including: containment, power, data, video and uplink 
commanding. Smoke was generated by overheating a 
small sample of material in the smoke generation duct 
for approximately 60 seconds. During this interval, 
controlled flow was induced by a moving piston in the 
aging chamber which drew the smoke into the chamber. 
The smoke was held in the aging chamber for a 
predetermined time, allowing the particles to coagulate. 
After a specified aging time, the smoke was then pushed 
by the piston into the diagnostics duct where the 
moment instruments made t heir measurements. Also 
installed in the diagnostics duct were space shuttle and 
ISS smoke detectors. As the smoke was monitored by 
the moment instruments, a sample of the smoke 
particles was deposited on a Transmission Electron 
Microscope (TEM) grid via a thermal precipitator which 
uses thermophoresis to deposit the particles on the 
grids. 
The zeroth and first moment devices showed good 
linearity over the conditions of interest however, the third 
moment device (TSI- DustTr ak®) is theoretically 
predicted to show non-monotonic behavior as particle 
size is increased. While a sa tisfactory prediction of the 
DustTrak® response was obtained using liquid droplets 
of dioctyl phthalate, the uncer tainty associated with the 
Mie scattering calculations due to the particle refractive 
index estimate, the potential of agglomerated particles, 
and deviation from assumed log-normal size distribution 
must be assessed further for the smoke samples here. 
In the results reported here, the DustTrak® response 
was directly calibrated, for each smoke source, against 
mass concentration measurements using a tapered 
element oscillating microbalance. This approach is valid 
as long as the size distribut ion of the sample does not 
change significantly. Using estimated material densities, 
the diameter of average mass was computed for each 
sample. Equation 7 was used to compute the geometric 
standard deviation from the ar ithmetic mean diameter 
and the diameter of aver age mass, and Equation 6 was 
used to compute the GMD.

EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS 
Overall, 30 sample materials were tested. These were 
comprised of six samples each of 5 materials: Teflon®, 
Kapton®, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and 
dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. Geometric 
Mean (GMD), Arithmetic Mean, and Average Mass 
diameters and the Geometric Standard Deviation (GSD) 
results from the moment in struments for baseline runs 
(no aging) and 720 second aging are presented in Table 
1. 
The Teflon® and Kapton® particles were very small with 
Teflon® showing limited increase in the size from the 
diameter of average mass co mpared to the arithmetic 
mean diameter. The lamp wick results exhibited 
substantially larger diamet er of average mass. As 
reported previously,11 the DustTrak results for lamp wick 
and silicone rubber demonstrated that substantial 
portions of the particle distribution possessed 
aerodynamic diameters larger than 1 micrometer. The 
small diameters for the Kapton® and Teflon® will make 
detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering 
devices; on the other hand, the large sizes seen with the 
lamp wick and silicone rubber would generate very large 
signals on a light scattering system, suggesting that 
detection of these particles against the background 
environment will require a detection system capable of 
measuring more than one moment of the particle size 
distribution. The aging re sults showed substantial 
increase in the average particle sizes with the diameter 
of average mass rising to over 500 nm for the aged 
silicone rubber. Since the aging process can be 
considered to be representative of smoke emerging from 
a closed volume (e.g. an avionics enclosure), fire 
sensors must consider large particles in addition to the 
smaller particles seen with Kapton®.

DETECTOR DESIGN REQUIREMENT IMPLICATIONS 
To develop requirements from these results, it is 
instructive to consider some basic overarching criteria: 
1. The requirement must not effectively define the 
technology 
2. The requirement must be verifiable in a laboratory. 
3. If the requirement describes or implies a test that 
cannot be done on every unit, it must be possible to 
define a subtest that can be conducted to qualify 
production units. 
4. The requirement should represent the best 
understanding of spacecraft smoke conditions. 
 
One possible method to meet these criteria is to develop 
a requirement that states an aerosol condition at alarm. 
To provide some perspective on the impact of the choice 
of such requirements, Figs. 3 and 4 present the outcome 
of a hypothetical single point requirement if it were

One possible method to meet these criteria is to develop 
a requirement that states an aerosol condition at alarm. 
To provide some perspective on the impact of the choice 
of such requirements, Figs. 3 and 4 present the outcome 
of a hypothetical single point requirement if it were 
implemented with different detector technologies. Each 
of these technologies respond to different particle 
characteristics such as the first or third moment of the 
distribution or the scattering signal. These figures were

geometric mean diameter (GMD) and a geometric 
standard deviation (GSD) of 1.3. The values for the 
moment devices were calculated using Eq. 6 and the 
values for the scattering device were calculated using 
the Mie scattering model of Gockel. 13 In practice, a fire 
could produce a smoke particle size distribution with a 
GMD different than 500 nm yet each of these detectors 
would have an alarm point determined by their response 
at the alarm-requirement aerosol. For each type of 
detector, the alarm number concentration (Fig. 3) or

function of the particle diameter. This is the

or large ends of the particle distribution. For example, 
as particle diameter is increased, progressively smaller

Similar dependencies are seen with all detectors 
suggesting that a detector that measures a single 
moment of the size distribution may suffer from 
conditions where it is either too sensitive or not sensitive 
enough. Consequently a specification for a single 
particle size (or no size specification) would be risky. If 
the requirement is limited to a single particle size, the 
result can easily be a detector that is insensitive to the 
other sizes. This is essent ially the case for the current 
ISS and STS detectors which are tuned to different size 
ranges and have very different sensitivities to particle 
size.5 An alternative is to develop alarm requirements 
that include criteria at particle sizes spanning the 
expected range of fire particulate (e.g. 200 to 1200 nm). 
A detector that involves two moment measurements 
may be able to capitalize on the size information that is 
generated by the ratio between the two moment values. 
As can be seen in Figs. 3 and 4, the systematic variation 
between the alarm signals of di fferent instruments could 
be used to discern size information This is similar to the 
approach suggested by Litton et al. who demonstrated 
that by combining two simple particle sensors that 
measure different moments, an inexpensive assessment 
of the particle size could be achieved. 14 With a detector 
that provides a combinat ion of a concentration or 
moment measurement and an indication of the size, it 
would be possible to satisfy detection requirements that 
include concentrations at more than one particle size 
and the two signals might also help reduce false alarms

Smoke particle size measurements were obtained under low-gravity conditions by 
overheating several materials typical of th ose found in spacecraf t. The measurements 
included integral measurements of the smoke pa rticles and physical sa mple of the particles 
for Transmission Electron Microscope analysis . The integral moments were combined to 
obtain geometric mean particle sizes and geometric standard deviations. These results are 
presented with the details of the instrument calibrations. The experimental results show 
that, for the materials tested, a substantial po rtion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm 
in diameter. 
I. Introduction 
ppropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to 
be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters. Terrestrial fire detection systems have been 
developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires. 1, 2 Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for 
spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial 
designs. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from 
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravit y increases the residence time in microgravity fires and 
increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector. 3 Microgravity fires have been found to have 
radically different structure from their 1-g counterparts. The limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire 
increase the importance of early detec tion. Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical 
terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previous ly evaluated. All of these effects can be expected to 
change the smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of 
smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors.
