III. Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 
45 flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, 
when an additional 17 flames were ignited. As such, a total of 62 flames were ignited in 
the first round of testing. Meanwhile, the BRE’s second-round flame testing began in 
Sept. 2020, during Increment 63, during which 47 flames were ignited. The second and 
final round of tests should be completed during Increment 64. 
 
The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable 
the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second 
round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. However, the break was longer than 
had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew 
availability. As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds 
of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was 
the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability 
would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than 
demonstration, phase. 
 
All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning 
ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range 
of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible 
crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was 
especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 
26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with 
nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) 
from preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 
82 
 
vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But during tests days, the atmosphere 
was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests. 
 
Second round testing is being carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 
and 50 mm, and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with 
nitrogen. Therefore, the second round of tests features a broader range of conditions 
than investigated during the first round. 
 
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed 
with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch 
for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and 
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of 
fuel concentrations. 
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all ISS results are 
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies 
There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increments 59 
and 63, but there was one in Increment 58 during the preparations for BRE testing 
(that was mistakenly not addressed in the 30-day report including that increment). It 
was discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle 
for the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle had 
been on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a 
nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and 
not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was 
replaced on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data 
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often 
saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment 
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own 
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors. Estimates had been made of 
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the 
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the 
radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The 
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been 
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted 
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 
times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer 
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were 
exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE 
testing continued unchanged.

and quickly became saturated. However, for some of the small size flames, these 
data were complete. Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and

Ignition was not always successful. As previously discussed, it was discovered on 1 
April 2019 (GMT 091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test 
day, preventing further flame testing until it could be replaced. While such

conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to 
momentary flashes without sustained ignition. Given that unplanned crew time is 
required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees - 
the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was 
known from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the

which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be

D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student 
Parham Dehghani) 
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers, 
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering 
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design 
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
All of the round 1 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their original 
calibrations. As presented below, the data is being processed to address the effect of the 
combustion product water condensation on the sensor surfaces.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 
88 
 
 
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from 
the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass 
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated 
fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of 
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in 
an inert matrix). Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real 
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this 
has not been shown before. 
 
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. 
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center (r = 9.5 mm). As the sensors 
are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion 
products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as the dew point 
for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature 
and can achieve temperatures over 100oC. Thus, condensation can occur at 
temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor. Above the 
dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor. When 
the sensor is dry and above 100oC, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases 
as intended. 
 
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with the 
duplicative NASA BRE burner. Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect 
in the ISS tests. The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully 
evaporates. More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect. Fortunately, by 
the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.

E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral 
student Parham Dehghani) 
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat 
surface of 25 mm diameter. Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have 
focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced 
wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be possible from normal-
gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets, 
has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many droplet flames were found to 
extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the extended 
ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal 
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia 
and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. These are 
all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft 
 
Figure 5 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred 
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a 
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done by using the arithmetic average 
of the center and offset heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux.

Let us interpret Figures 14 and 15 in terms of the flammability of real materials in 
microgravity. Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to 
3 kJ/g, with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g. Some

2 [1] using the Cone Calorimeter can measure these material properties. As this study

I. Introduction 
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity 
Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically, 
BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as 
extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the 
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments. A flat 
porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where 
measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the 
vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent. A small number of gaseous fuels (including 
mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 
109 
 
alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface 
temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that 
directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an 
efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire-
resistant spacecraft materials. 
 
BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA 
does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B. 
J. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 
ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-
considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % 
oxygen; 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can 
be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 
K. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 
L. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. 
The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e., 
liquids and non-charring plastics). 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. 
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity 
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
 
II. Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. 
The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most 
common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and 
the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 
110 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the 
NASA Glenn Research Center. The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in 
a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it could 
alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control 
parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in 
the telemetry stream. For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady 
data has been collected. But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far 
for BRE or ACME in general. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 
 
 
III. Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 
45 flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, 
when an additional 17 flames were ignited. BRE’s second-round flame testing began in 
Sept. 2020, during Increment 63, in which 47 flames were ignited. The second and final 
round of tests was completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames 
were ignited. As a result, 62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and 
second rounds of testing for a total of 194 flames. 
 
The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable 
the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second 
round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. However, the break was longer than 
had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew 
availability. As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds 
of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was 
the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability 
would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than 
demonstration, phase. 
 
All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning 
ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range 
of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible 
crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was 
especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 
26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 
111 
 
nitrogen and any combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from 
preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was 
vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But during tests days, the atmosphere 
was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests. 
Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and 
50 mm, and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen. 
Therefore, the second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than 
investigated during the first round. However, in contrast to the first round most of the 
round 2 tests were carried out at roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary 
effect on flames. Meanwhile, the tests in this round were carried out at various oxygen 
concentrations as in the first round but were more often conducted with ~40% oxygen, 
where oxygen of course has a strong effect on combustion. 
 
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed 
with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch 
for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and 
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of 
fuel concentrations. 
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all ISS results are 
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments.

1. Mission anomalies 
There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increments 59 
and 63, but there was one in Increment 58 during the preparations for BRE testing 
(that was mistakenly not addressed in the 30-day report including that increment). It 
was discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle 
for the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle had

been on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a 
nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and 
not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was

The anomaly in Increment 64 was similar in that there was a slow leak of the GCIP’s

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data 
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often 
saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment 
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own 
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors. Estimates had been made of 
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the 
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the 
radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The 
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been 
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted 
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 
times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer 
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were 
exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE 
testing continued unchanged during the first round, i.e., during increments 58 and 59.

The 194 flames ignited for BRE significantly exceeds the 73 tests which were specified as

It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not necessarily available for

per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some 
image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This 
is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the 
project constraints. 
 
From BRE Co-I Peter Sunderland: 
The video and image data of the testing produced satisfactory data to display the 
nature of the burning sequence from ignition to self-extinction or fuel termination. 
However, the image quality is less than was hoped for. The ACME ops camera 
provides video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, and for many flames it is

D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student 
Parham Dehghani; lightly edited by Dennis Stocker) 
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers, 
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering 
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design 
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
All of the round 1 and 2 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their 
original calibrations. As presented below, the data is being processed to address the 
effect of the combustion product water condensation on the sensor surfaces. 
 
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from 
the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass 
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated 
fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of 
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in 
an inert matrix). Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real 
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this 
has not been shown before. 
 
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. 
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center (r = 9.5 mm). As the sensors 
are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion 
products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as the dew point 
for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature 
and can achieve temperatures over 100oC. Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures 
below the dew point that lead to added heat to the sensor. Above the dew point, the 
condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor. When the sensor is 
dry and above 100oC, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended. 
 
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with the 
duplicative NASA BRE burner. Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect 
in the ISS tests. The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully 
evaporates. More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect. Fortunately, by

E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral 
student Parham Dehghani; lightly edited by Dennis Stocker) 
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat 
surface of 25 mm diameter. Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have 
focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced 
wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be possible from normal-
gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets, 
has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many droplet flames were found to 
extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the extended 
ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal 
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia 
and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. These are 
all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft 
 
Figure 6 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred 
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a 
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done by using the arithmetic average 
of the center and offset heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux.

The experimental flammability maps are shown in Figures 15 and 16. Both plots indicate 
a decreasing, inverse asymptotic-like curve that approaches zero, for heat of gasification 
with mass flux. It is surprising that the data cluster about a nearly singular trend. 
However, both plots show that the heat of gasification is up to 20 % higher for the lower 
heat of combustion 23.6 kJ/g. Our tests in the University of Maryland lab have shown, 
with the BRE in 1-g that similar results for propane-nitrogen mixtures have the opposite 
behavior with heats of gasification decreasing with heat of combustion for the same mass 
flux. But again, the data mostly cluster about one trend line except for very low heats of 
combustion. However, the corresponding 1-g heat of combustion data shift far to the 
right and down from the microgravity data of Figures 15 and 16. For example, the 1-g 
data would indicate ( 𝑚̇ ”, 𝐿) points of about 30 g/m2s, 2 kJ/g and 10, 0.5. Moreover, our 
previous work in a 5- s drop facility suggested similar data trends but with an apparent 
vertical asymptote at about 3 g/m2s, rather than 1 as shown here. Obviously, the current 
data at durations of minutes are more accurate than those limited to 5 s. However, it has 
been shown that the ISS heat flux data even at self-extinction are theoretically nearly 
steady. Figures 15 and 16 include the heats of gasification derived from the self-
extinguished endpoint data as well. Remarkably, the self-extinguished not-so-steady data 
follow the same trend as the steady data. 
 
Let us interpret Figures 15 and 16 in terms of the flammability of real materials in 
microgravity. Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to 
3 kJ/g, with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g. Some 
selected literature values for materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are 
listed in Table 4. The accuracy of the calorimeter heat flux is found to be less than the 
two sensors, thus, we relied on the arithmetic average of the two heat flux sensors data 
for obtaining the flammability map. However, same results are shown considering the 
calorimeter data. Figure 15 would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) 
would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s. Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5 
g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.

On GMT 039, we performed our first ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points. Unlike the other 
ACME experiments, BRE is focused on improving spacecraft fire safety rather than practical terrestrial 
combustion. More specifically, BRE uses gaseous fuels to determine the flammability of liquids and solids 
in microgravity by selecting test conditions to match key parameters. We performed nine successful tests 
burning ethylene on the 25-mm diameter burner, where the burner’s embedded sensors measure the 
heat flux that would normally vaporize a liquid or solid fuel. The tests were conducted under a range of 
oxygen concentrations and pressures, including some atmospheres that could be used for future crew 
vehicles or habitats.

Figure 1 shows a sequence of three images from BRE’s first on-orbit test. The first image shows that the 
flame grew to become nominally hemispherical (over the burner outlet, which can also be seen). The 
second image shows a hole in the top of the flame due to radiative heat loss. However, the third image

shows that the flame recovered, where the hole closed. In this latter phase of the test, measurements of 
chemiluminescence (from OH*) clearly reveal that the flame was oscillating at approximately 1 Hz. These 
oscillations (the opening and closing of the flame’s top) were seen to grow in magnitude and are 
associated with the flame’s approach to extinction. In the first test, this lasted for an extended time, but 
in other tests at lower oxygen concentrations the oscillations sometimes lasted 10 seconds or less before 
the flame quenched. BRE seeks to understand the flame extinction and the conditions under which the 
flames become unsteady and finally extinguish. 
 
Week 21: February 15-21 
Testing for the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment resumed on GMT 051 following a revision of the 
ignition procedure. Eight successful tests were conducted burning pure ethylene, which is naturally a 
sooty fuel because of its double bond, but the soot produced during ignition quickly vanished leaving a 
pale blue flame, where the flame temperatures were insufficient to generate soot. These flames grow to 
be nominally hemispherical, then become quasi-steady although weakening, and finally become unsteady 
and extinguish when radiative heat losses become too great. The experiment’s goal is to improve our 
understanding of material flammability in microgravity and thereby guide the selection of materials use 
in spacecraft.

momentarily just a ring. At the end, before complete extinction, the flame also partially detaches 
from the burner, leaving a crack in the flame’s side extending from the base to its top.

Ignition, extinction, and the three main phases of the BRE flame’s life can be seen in this example plot of 
the OH* chemiluminescence measured by one of the three PhotoMultipiler Tube (PMT) modules on the 
ACME Chamber Insert. OH* is an excited molecule that loses energy by emitting a photon of light at a 
specific wavelength (in the ultraviolet). In combustion of most fuels, there is oxygen, hydrogen, and lots 
of energy making OH* measurements a good indicator of the flame. 
 
This data shows that the flame is weakening during the quasi-steady period when the flame size and shape 
is nominally constant. The OH* measurement also clearly shows the oscillations that precede extinction 
and their growing strength. The flame’s oscillations (e.g., with the opening and closing of the top) are at 
a nominally constant frequency that is a little less than 1 Hz. The huge OH* oscillations are the flame’s 
death throes when it splits open from bottom to top and partially detaches from the burner.

The test shown in this video is the first ACME test—of all the experiments thus far—to have such 
a high fuel flow rate. Initially, the flame behavior is similar to previous BRE tests. The flame is very 
sooty at ignition, due to ethylene’s double bond, where you can see the glowing soot particles

the natural color of hydrocarbon flames. The flame expands to reach enough oxygen to consume 
the fuel. Meanwhile, the flame is blanketed by a thickening cloud of carbon dioxide and water

weakens, and radiative heat loss leaves a hole in the flame. But oxygen then mixes with the fuel,

and closing grows in strength as in previous tests, but the flame size is apparently so large that 
asymmetries begin. The flame eventually becomes mostly quenched with just a ring at the base 
and a highly dynamic spiral extending upward. As in previous tests, the flame partially detaches 
from the burner (right side of video), but in this case, the flame surprisingly persists for roughly 
20 seconds despite the large-scale detachment. While careful analysis will be challenging, this 
flame is visually dramatic with its swirling pulsations and powerful death throes.

flames during each test’s duration. If the test durations weren’t limited, these flames would have 
eventually gone out, but it could have taken many minutes for that to happen.

On GMT 247, we began the second round of testing for ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) with 13 flames

In many of these 50-mm burner tests, heat loss caused the top of the flame to locally quench—creating a

were “chasing its tail.”

On GMT 352, ten nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames were ignited for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) 
experiment. Ethylene’s (C2H4) C=C double bond can create sooty flames. These tests were conducted in 
oxygen concentrations ranging between 32% to 40%. BRE’s goal is to improve our understanding of 
material flammability in microgravity and thereby guide the selection of materials used in spacecraft.

CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
Upon ignition, the ethylene flame in this video clip exhibits a lot of soot, which is bright whitish-
yellow in appearance. On Earth, soot is normally consumed as it passes through the flame sheet, 
but in this test point the soot particles are large enough to escape the flame. In microgravity, soot 
growth can be enhanced because it stays within the flame longer due to the absence of buoyancy. 
Despite this enhanced residence time, the soot fades away quickly as the burn continues. High 
temperatures are required to create the soot and microgravity conditions can lead to lower flame 
temperatures. There is no buoyancy to bring in fresh oxygen and the combustion products blanket 
these low-momentum flames. The carbon dioxide, water vapor, and soot contribute to radiative 
heat loss. This video clip ends as the flame becomes mostly blue and soot-free. 
 
Week 11: December 25 - 31 
On GMT 358, 17 ethylene flames were ignited for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) experiment. 
These tests were conducted in oxygen concentrations ranging from 24% to 40%, and the ethylene fuel 
was generally diluted with nitrogen. At the higher oxygen concentrations, the flames were generally quasi-
steady and continued to burn until the fuel was shut off. In contrast, at the lower oxygen concentrations, 
the flames all self-extinguished. On GMT 364, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov replaced the gas bottle at CIR 
Manifold #2 to support continuation of ACME BRE test points.

ACME BRE Graph 
 
 
This graph shows as a function of time, the fuel flow (red) and three optical flame measurements from a 
test in which pure ethylene was burned. The optical flame measurements were made with 
Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules of OH* chemiluminescence (purple), CH* chemiluminescence (light 
blue), and broadband emissions in the visible and near UV spectrum (dark blue). OH* and CH* are 
transient molecules which, in the process of chemiluminescence, emit a photon at specific wavelengths 
when they drop to a lower energy level. The CH* chemiluminescence is the principal source of the blue 
seen in hydrocarbon flames, while OH* is in the ultraviolet and is used in ACME to indicate ignition and 
extinction. 
 
The initially sooty flame was ignited at 32 seconds, after which the hot-wire igniter was retracted. At about 
60 seconds, after the ceramic fiber array was inserted, the flame became quasi-steady. But the PMT 
signals weakened with time, where the low-momentum flame became increasingly blanketed by carbon 
dioxide and water vapor in the absence of buoyancy. 
 
At about 95 seconds, the increasing radiative loss caused the flame’s top to quench, creating a hole in the 
flame. This hole allowed the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, to directly mix. 
This mixing enhanced flammability, and the flame quickly reestablished and closed the hole, but then 
again, it locally quenched. This oscillatory behavior happened repeatedly at roughly 1 Hz with the flame 
opening growing with time until the flame became just a ring. We saw this phenomenon in the first round 
of BRE testing performed on ISS in 2019. A paper about computational modeling of it is now in press. 
 
At about 135 seconds, the flame began to partially detach from the rim of the burner and then reattach 
until it completely extinguished at 148 seconds.

Week 14: January 15 - 21 
In support of ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, Victor Glover removed the broken fiber and

ignited for the ACME BRE experiment. The array of ceramic fibers (now with three instead of five

and habitats, where that included elevated oxygen concentrations and reduced pressures which can 
facilitate EVA preparation. At normal atmospheric conditions (e.g., ~21% oxygen by volume), the flames 
all self-extinguished. In contrast, three of the five tests conducted at 30-35% oxygen and 0.57 bar (i.e., 8.2 
psia) featured quasi-steady flames, which continued to burn through the test duration. While the oxygen 
concentration dominates the flame behavior, this day’s tests will enable a better understanding of the 
role of the atmospheric pressure on microgravity flammability. On GMT 021, Kate Rubins replaced the gas 
bottles at CIR Manifold #2 and CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of ACME BRE test points.

In support of ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, Kate Rubins replaced the burner in the ACME 
Chamber Insert on GMT 025. In contrast to the 25-mm burner that was removed, this burner is 50 mm in 
diameter and allows for larger flames. Tests are being conducted with this larger burner to investigate the 
dependence of the microgravity flammability on flame size. 
 
Week 16: January 29 – February 4 
On GMT 028, the final test points were performed for the ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) experiment 
led by researchers from the University of Maryland and Russia’s Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic 
University. In the study of microgravity flammability, 13 flames were ignited with the 50-mm diameter 
burner at oxygen concentrations from 40% to 23% in 1 atm. This larger burner allows for larger flames 
compared to the 25-mm burner that was used for previous tests. Generally, these larger flames tended 
to self-extinguish due to radiative heat loss, which scales with the flame size. In contrast, the smaller 
flames on the 25-mm burner were generally quasi-steady. BRE studies material flammability with the goal 
of improving spacecraft fire safety.

extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted, especially under conditions where 
the flame is sooty or could become unstable. The results could lead to the improved design of practical 
combustion devices on Earth.

This clip from a test point video shows a flame’s oscillatory “death throes” leading ultimately to 
the flame’s extinction (not shown in the clip). Initially, radiative heat loss causes the top of the 
flame (on the video’s left) to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. That opening allows the 
fuel (from the burner) and oxygen (in the chamber) to directly mix, which increases the 
flammability and causes the flame to reestablish. But, due to heat loss, the flame partially 
quenches again, and the opening grows with each oscillation cycle. Later, the flame also begins to 
detach from the burner’s rim, leaving an opening at the flame’s base (on the video’s right). Here 
too the flame reestablishes but then opens again—the opening growing until it extends from the

Appendix N. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The BRE data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other 
ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground. 
 
The BRE image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, typically used with a CH* filter (and likely always or nearly always for BRE) 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and 
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was 
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

Recommended Action Closure Rationale 
There are no warnings to 
eliminate damage to the 
test hardware 
To minimize the likelihood of 
hardware damage, the flight & 
ground software designs 
should incorporate software 
requirements to identify invalid 
commands and command 
parameters that are outside of 
allowable limits and to alert 
operations personnel that 
invalid commands were 
entered. 
 
A complete software command list for the ACME hardware has 
been derived from operational requirements for the ACME 
system. Operational limits have been defined for each 
command and incorporated into the software requirement set. 
The software requirements are documented in the Software 
section of the ACME Engineering Requirements Document 
(ERD) ACME-REQ-001. 
This list of signals is also documented in the ACME Data 
Dictionary Document (ACME-DOC-008). 
These documents will be available for NASA review and 
comment during the CDR. 
The approved operational limitations will be built into the 
ACME ground command station software at the TSC. Every 
command sent by an operator will be checked against these 
established limits. Commands that violate safe ranges will be 
rejected (on the ground) and the operator will receive an error 
message. This ground software will be verified, as part of the 
overall ACME test and verification campaign, to ensure no 
command can ever reach the ACME hardware that is outside 
of these safely established limits.

STD-ACME-1 17.a) where the volume has a stored energy < 3,063 ft-
lbs. Volumes with a stored energy > 3,063 ft-lbs will have a depress 
rate calculated. 
 
• Depress rates are calculated* for each volume to show that the 
volume’s depress rate is greater than maximum station / vehicle 
depress rate so no pressure load is generated 
• Maximum depress rate is defined in section 3.1.1.2.1.5 part B of SSP-
50835 Rev C as 13.3kPa/s (1.93psi/sec) 
 
 
 
*AIAA Journal, October 1986, Vol. 24, No. 10, pg 1709-1711, “Formulas for Venting or Charging 
Gas from a Single Volume”, H.T. Yang

• Risk Title: IPSU to IOP image transfer rates take too long 
• Risk Statement: Given that the current data transfer rates from the IPSU 
to the IOP is severely limited, transfer of ACME data may take an 
unacceptable amount of time and may reduce obtainable science for the 
allotted operational time on board ISS. 
• Likelihood: 4 
• Consequence: 3 
• Approach: Watch. Need to keep an eye on this and follow up 
with the CIR team to keep updated on transfer improvements. 
• Latest Status: 09/17/13 - The IPSU-G is going to have their 
PDR September 26th 2013. The IPSU-G will eliminate 
the need to transfer image data from an IPSU to the IOP for downlink 
because the IPSU-G will be able to directly downlink image data to 
the ground. A trigger for this risk would be the cancellation of the 
IPSU-G project that would require ACME to mitigate, accept, etc...

Title: Overpressurization of CIR pressurized system by ISS Nitrogen 
Supply 
Description: Overpressurization of the CIR pressurized system by 
the ISS nitrogen supply via the CIR nitrogen bypass line results in 
rupture of CIR hardware, damage to ISS hardware or injury to the 
crew.

pressure relief valve for the CIR nitrogen bypass line, and will be 
set at 135 psia.

overpressurization due to the ISS nitrogen gas supply. See CIR 
Hazard Report FCF-C10, hazard controls, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6 and 3.8.

FCF-ACME-04 
Title: Adiabatic Combustion Ruptures CIR Combustion Chamber or CIR Exhaust 
Vent Package during ACME experiments (except for the Inverse Flame Experiment) 
Description: Rapid overpressurization during the combustion of ACME gaseous 
fuel and oxidizer/diluent exceeds the MDP of the CIR Combustion chamber and/or 
exhaust vent package resulting in damage to CIR or ISS hardware or injury to the 
crew. 
Note (on hazard report): 
1. This hazard report works in conjunction with CIR hazard report FCF-C07, “Adiabatic Combustion 
ruptures the chamber walls, causing damage to station and/or injury to crew.“ Overpressurization due 
to combustion will be controlled by limiting the fuel volume in each gas bottle. The CIR Valve Timers 
will be placed in the fuel mode. The chamber will be pre-filled with gaseous oxidizer and gaseous fuel 
will flow through the ACME burner. 
2. CIR is responsible for filling the experiment gas bottles. The ACME detonation analyses determine the 
limits on fuel volumes in each bottle. The fuel gas volumes will be chosen such that even if the entire 
contents of a bottle were to be released into the CIR Combustion Chamber, any adiabatic combustion 
would result in a pressure less than the MDP of the CIR Combustion chamber. The MDP of the CIR 
chamber is 135 psia. 
3. The CIR bottle leakage hazard controls and verifications are covered in CIR hazard report FCF-C08 
Leakage of Pressurized System. 
4. The CIR system rupture hazard controls and verifications are covered in CIR hazard report FCF-C10 
Rupture of Pressurized Systems.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
 
PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research. The 
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant 
emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary 
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. 
 
RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiments 
investigating laminar, gaseous, non-premixed flames. They 
are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International 
Space Station (ISS). 
STATUS: ACME set-up and check-out was carried out by the 
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017, where science testing began in 
November. The first round of testing for the Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment of Marshall B. Long 
et al. was completed in Feb. 2018, where 130 methane 
flames (at a range of concentrations) were ignited. The first 
round of testing for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment of Derek 
Dunn-Rankin et al. was completed on May 18, where 120 
coflow flames were ignited. On May 20, burners and 
additional hardware for the next three ACME experiments 
are scheduled to launch. The ACME hardware should be 
reconfigured on May 22 by astronaut Ricky Arnold (NASA) 
for CLD Flame’s second round, where the ethylene flame 
testing should begin later in the week.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
 
PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research. The 
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant 
emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary 
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. 
 
RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiments 
investigating laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels. 
The experiments are being conducted with a single set of 
modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) 
on the International Space Station (ISS). While the ISS 
astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests 
are remotely commanded from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center. 
STATUS: ACME setup and checkout were carried out by the 
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017. Thus far, a dozen astronauts 
from Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States 
have supported the ACME research. Since November 2017, 
over 300 flames have been ignited for the Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) and Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiments led 
respectively by Profs. Marshall B. Long (Yale University) and 
Derek Dunn-Rankin (University of California, Irvine). 
 
A second round of CLD Flame tests is currently underway and 
should end in September when the testing will transition 
back to the E-FIELD Flames experiment. In late 2018, the 
hardware will be reconfigured for the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) experiment led by Prof. Jim Quintiere (University of 
Maryland). While the first two ACME experiments are 
focused on improving practical combustion on Earth, BRE is 
aimed at improving spacecraft fire safety.

Lifted flames (detached from the burner) as a function of the 
matched fuel and air velocity from the CLD Flame experiment. 
The false color indicates the CH* concentration as function of 
the radius and height above the burner. CH* is an excited 
species and emits blue light as it drops to a lower energy level in 
a process known as chemiluminescence. It is the primary source 
of the blue that is the natural color of hydrocarbon flames 
(neglecting the broadband thermal radiation from the soot). 
Diffusion flames with a weak air coflow as a function of the electric field strength, where an open copper mesh above the flame is 
negatively and positively charged in the top and bottom rows, respectively. Flames naturally include ions which can be affected 
by a powerful electric or magnetic field. In ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment, the copper mesh is energized up to 10,000 volts. 
This technology could be used to stabilize fuel-lean flames under conditions which are less polluting.

INTRODUCTION 
 
Science Summary 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under 
development with a set of five independent experiments which are each focused on advancing 
combustion technology through fundamental research. Four of the current ACME experiments 
are specifically directed at addressing energy and environmental concerns, while the fifth 
experiment addresses fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. The overall goals are to improve 
our understanding of materials flammability, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both 
optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, flame stability and extinction limits, 
soot control and reduction, oxygen enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon 
sequestration, and the use of electric fields for combustion control. 
 
While distinct, the ACME experiments share several significant traits. The principal unifying 
feature of the experiments is their use of gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than 
liquid or solid fuels. With this in common, the experiments will be conducted within the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) through the use of a single modular insert. In addition to the 
fuel state, the current set of ACME experiments all use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) 
flames for their studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are either one or two dimensional, 
depending upon the experiment. 
 
With the exception of the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment discussed immediately 
below, the general goal of the current ACME experiments is to gain fundamental understanding 
that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on 
Earth, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and 
transport processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced performance, 
improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design. 
In summary, microgravity investigations of non-premixed flames could lead to eco-friendly 
combustion systems providing our nation with green power for the future. 
 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) 
Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is 
focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraf t. Specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve 
our fundamental understanding of materials flamma bility, such as extinction behavior and the 
conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability 
test methods for low and partial-gravity envir onments. A flat porous burner fed with gaseous 
fuel will simulate the burning of solid and liqui d fuels, where measurements are made of the 
thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon whic h the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels 
depend.

Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) 
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our 
current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, 
namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. The general goal of 
the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame 
conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical 
kinetic and soot formation submodels. The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection 
velocity and fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly 
sooting conditions. Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene 
flames in an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be directly applicable 
to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result 
of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the 
flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant 
emission. The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD 
Flames) experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and 
investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames. Outside reviewers 
concluded that the experiment “… will contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge 
of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted 
with a simple gas-jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage 
(up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) 
the burner. Measurements, as a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of the 
ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
Flame Design 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot 
inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the 
“design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. An outside review panel 
declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient 
and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and 
extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame 
experiment.

the 
“design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. An outside review panel 
declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient 
and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and 
extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame 
experiment. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene 
or methane) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot 
inception. The effect of the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both 
normal flames and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from 
the spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will explore 
whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for 
non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for 
premixed flames.

Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) 
The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment is to 
advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free 
and sooty flames. The spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity, will be created 
through use of a porous spherical burner from which a fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the 
CIR chamber. Flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition 
naturally toward extinction. Tests will be conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel 
and chamber atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane for soot-free flames, 
and ethylene for sooty flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for 
both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, 
respectively). Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating 
instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent 
mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

1.10. Ignition 
While hot-wire igniters have been effectivel y used in many combustion experiments, 
special care is required for ACME because of the testing with elevated oxygen (for 
the Flame Design experiment) which leads to higher flame temperatures which in 
turn could significantly shorten igniter life . Hot Surface Ignition (HSI), which is 
often used in furnaces, may be better for ACME than hot-wire ignition. 
1.10.1. The igniter shall reliably ignite all initia l flow conditions. Reliable ignition shall 
be verified in 1g at the limiting (i.e., extreme) conditions in the test matrices for 
each burner within 1 s of igniter activation. For the spherical and BRE burners, 
it is suggested that the ignition occur at about 3 mm from the burner outlet. For 
the gas-jet, coflow, and BRE burners, the i gnition should occur within the mixing 
layer between the fuel and oxidizer (and not centered on the burner axis).3,4,* 
1.10.2. Hydrodynamic disturbance from igniter insertion and retraction shall be 
minimized by inserting the igniter at least 30 s prior to ignition, and removing it 
from the free area within 0.5 s after igniti on detection. The igniter retraction time 
is a required example, where it shall be po ssible to vary that time as described in 
ACME’s Science Operations Requirements Document (SORD). The disturbance 
can be minimized through a linear rath er than a sweeping retraction, and by 
limiting the speed of the retraction (because a rapid retraction could disturb the 
flame). 
1.10.3. The igniter energy output shall be variable and minimized to ensure minimal 
effects on subsequent flame behavior and avoid igniter burnout. As one example 
of implementation, the igniter should not be energized longer than required.3,* 
1.10.4. The capability to vary the ignition dura tion and set it to an uplinked value 
between 0 and 10 s is required.*

4. Operational Requirements 
The general science requirements are now co mbined in ACME’s Science Operations 
Requirements Document (SORD), but this does not eliminate the importance of this section 
of the existing ISRD in describing the ge neral operational sequences. However, these 
operational sequences should be considered as examples where the details are subject to 
change. For example, future ground-based or ISS testing may reveal that superior results 
are achieved when the igniter is prehea ted before the gas flows are initiated. The times 
specified in the ISRD shall also be consid ered as required examples, where it shall be 
possible to vary those times as described in the SORD. Furthermore, it should be 
understood that the sequences in the ISRD don’t fully address operational details associated 
with measurements, e.g., the position or range of positions for the Thin Filament Pyrometry 
(TFP). It should also be understood that the form at of this ISRD section is not consistent 
between experiments, especially in regard to description of the pre-ignition and post-
extinction steps. 
 
4.1. CLD Flame 
The main goal of this experiment is to eva luate flame characteristics at the extremes 
of fuel dilution: both weak, highly-dilute flames, and sooting flames up to pure-fuel 
conditions. While such parameters as the extin ction limits and potential smoke points 
within these flames can easily be determin ed in normal gravity, we will not know the 
exact microgravity limits until the experiment is run on the ISS. We therefore plan to 
execute an initial run for each fuel where we vary the flow velocities and dilution 
levels in order to determine the extinc tion limits and degree of soot production in 
microgravity. For extinction limits, the flow velocity will be slowly ramped until 
extinction is observed for a given dilution level. The dilution level will then be 
increased in 5% increments and the proce dure repeated. Extinction can be detected 
quickly with a PMT, but the color imagi ng system, HiBMs camera, and ops imaging 
system will all be run during these scans to maximize the data collected. For sooting 
determination, the dilution level will be decr eased in 5% increments and/or the flow 
velocity will be increased in 5 cm/s in crements until soot is observed, and then 
continued until either a smoke point is reached or a predetermined upper limit is 
reached. These observations can be made using the ops and color imaging systems. 
The table below outlines the procedure to determine the extinction limits of the 
flames as well as identify any smoke points for the C 2H4 flames. Based on the results 
of these scans, the exact test matrix can be modified as necessary for further runs.

specifically when changing the ratio of fuel to inert. To minimize this time, the 
mixture ratio will be held fixed and the ex it velocity will be varied. Varying the exit 
velocity has been observed to produce a steady flame within seconds. This 
improvement allows for data acquisition on the next test condition to begin without

moderately-dilute (or healthy) flame range for ignition purposes. The fuel dilution 
will be adjusted to the initial test case (if necessary) and then data acquisition will be 
carried out at the different fluid veloc ities until extinction is detected. Once the 
extinction limit is reached for a particular dilution level, the flow conditions will be 
reset to a healthy ignition setting and reignited.

4.2. E-FIELD Flames 
The E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objec tives corresponding to 4 series of tests 
using 2 different diffusion flame burner con figurations. The first three test series 
provide the key fundamental information regarding the electrical character of 
diffusion flames and the influence of electric fie lds on soot formation; the final series 
focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames. 
General Operations 
Before any of the electric field experiments, the high voltage mesh should be installed 
(or moved into position). Leak current s hould be measured by sweeping the voltage 
from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV with no flam e present. A steep rise in current under 
these conditions indicates corona discharg e and sets the upper limit on the potential. 
The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep with no flame to provide 
a point-by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep should be completed 
following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. Only ion current would need 
to be measured during the no-flame sweep. In addition, excessive leak current at 
relatively low voltage may indicate elect ron emission from carbon buildup on the gas 
jet flame tip. If the leak current exceeds 10% of the flame ion current, cleaning of the 
gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual wiping or possibly burning off 
the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be a rare request, but 
the continuous monitor of flameless ion cu rrent provides a reliable in-situ monitor. 
We assume that the chamber will be emp tied and refilled approximately every 7-8 
tests to minimize the oxygen concentration uncer tainty in the test chamber. The exact 
times for settling and voltage steps may vary (they should be reconfigurable from the 
ground), but a nominal expected operational sequence for one chamber fill and the 
key measurement data sets are shown below. 
 
 (A) Voltage Sweep – collection of VI curves (or VCC curves) -- where the voltage is 
swept from 0-±5kV (or until flame blowout) and the ion current is monitored and 
recorded. The sweep will consist of a series of discrete steps, where a settling time is 
allowed after each voltage change. At the same time, color and OH* video records 
the flame shape and luminosity (both broadband flame and soot luminosity and OH* 
chemiluminescence) throughout the sweep. A typical step sweep might comprise: 15 
second ignition & stabilization; 100 V/step, 0.3 sec settle between steps, and a 0.25 
sec. ion current measurement at each point, to ±5kV or blowout. Blowout can be 
detected by a sharp drop in ion current. Expected run time is 50 seconds per sweep 
(not including a background current sweep with the flame off). However, the time 
between voltage steps for flame adjustment and data collection shall be adjustable via 
uplink between the values of 0-10 seconds.

5. Test Matrices 
ACME’s combined test matrix (which is a spreadsheet) largely duplicates this section of the 
ISRD. Although an effort was made to limit th e required test matrices to a maximum of 
about 50 tests (i.e., ignitions) - or alternately 50 minutes of flame - per experiment, there was 
no target established for the highly desired or de sired tests. As a result, there is a large 
variation between the number of these tests between experiments and a large number of such 
tests overall. The initial chamber pressure is specified in both atmospheres and bar in the 
current ISRD, whereas it should be consistently in atmospheres for all tests. For example, 
where the ISRD specifies 1 bar, it should be interpreted as 1 atmosphere even though the two 
pressures are slightly different. 
 
5.1. CLD Flame 
Once the full range of flow conditions to i nvestigate has been determined using the 
initial exploratory procedure to establish extinction and sooting smoke-point limits, 
the plan for additional test cases will be finalized. Test matrices detailing the range of

The test matrices presented above were created with two goals in mind: to investigate 
weak, dilute flames as they approach extinction, and to investigate the sooting 
tendencies of richer flames. In all cases, flames are lifted off the burner surface so 
that heat transfer to the burner can be ne glected in the computations. This approach 
has been observed to work well for all cases of the methane flames, whereas 
moderate heating of the burner surface has been observed for some cases of the 
ethylene flames. The laminar flame speed of ethylene is higher than that of methane, 
causing lift-off heights to decrease by appr oximately a factor of two. For nonsooting 
flames, this decrease in lift-off height doe s not create any burner heating. However, 
the more heavily sooting cases have been observed to cause moderate heat transfer to 
the burner, which becomes a problem in th e ethylene flames since they have a higher 
propensity to soot, particularly at microgravity. The 50% C 2H4 / 50% N 2 flame has 
been observed to be the lowest level of dilution that ensures the room temperature 
boundary condition at the burner surfa ce to be a good assumption for the 
computations. By increasing the fuel flow rate by a factor of 2 (a s shown in Test #’s 
106-111 in Table 5.1.5), the overall amount of soot and the size of the sooting region 
are increased (at 1 g), with the sooting region substantially higher off the burner 
surface to prevent burner heating. Raising the sooting region further off the burner 
surface becomes more important under micr ogravity conditions as the lift-off height 
decreases relative to 1 g conditions due to the increased importance of axial 
diffusion.

5.4. s-Flame 
The three-part test matrix below is desi gned to meet the complete success criteria, 
addressing all scientific objectives listed above. 
All experimental sets will address transient phenomenon, as the flame evolves from 
localized ignition towards “steady” be havior, corresponding to Objective ( A). The 
flames evolve in a quasi-steady state manne r (becoming history independent), after a 
short initial transient. 
The rationale for this test matrix is to utilize various mixtures to assess both chemical 
and transport effects (including radiative) on flame behavior. Pure H 2 and pure CH4 
are utilized to assess kinetic mechanisms a ssociated with each. Additionally, pure H 2 
only produces H2O as its radiative product, thereby isolating its radiative properties. 
Mixtures composed of both H2 and CH4 are used to examine their combined chemical 
and transport effects. Various inerts which affect characteristic flame temperature 
and transport (molecular and radiative), all in the same mole fractions, are utilized 
for comparison. C 2H4 allows for the examination of a fuel with nominal unity Le 
number. Additionally, its characteristic sooting nature directly addresses our basic 
science objectives focusing on ( A) spreading of flame sheets, ( B) dual extinction 
states, and (C) flamefront instabilities. 
The fuel/inert mixtures in the REQUI RED experiment sets 1-2 include H 2/CH4 
mixtures (see subsets a, b, c) and H 2 and CH4 as pure fuels (see subsets d, e) aimed at 
addressing chemical kinetic aspects. The inert mole fractions are all fixed at 55% for 
baseline comparison. As can be seen, the d ifference between sets 1 and 2 is the inert 
(N2 versus He), which is chosen to assess transport (e.g. diffusive properties) effects 
on flame stability. For example, experimental set 2 is aimed at inducing the pulsating 
instability for Le > 1, corresponding to Obj ective ©. The fuel components and their 
relative compositions are the same for sets 1-2, with different inert species in 
balance; similarly, the ambient compositi on reflects the use of a different inert 
species in the fuel mixture. It is noted that the characteristic flame temperatures 
(which will affect the Zeldovich number, Ze) will be different for the two experimental 
sets affecting stability and extinction. 
Experiment sets 1-2 will also assess radia tive extinction for high flow rates (see i, ii, 
iii under the flow rate category) and kinetic extinction for low flow rates (see iv and v 
under the flow rate category), corresponding to Objective ( B). With regard to 
radiative extinction, mixture compositions of 25%H 2/20%CH4, 20%H2/25%CH4, and 
30%H2/15%CH4 have been shown in drop-tower expe riments to be characterized by 
different radiative extinction times. These mixtures also eschew sooty ignition (due to

ate category) and kinetic extinction for low flow rates (see iv and v 
under the flow rate category), corresponding to Objective ( B). With regard to 
radiative extinction, mixture compositions of 25%H 2/20%CH4, 20%H2/25%CH4, and 
30%H2/15%CH4 have been shown in drop-tower expe riments to be characterized by 
different radiative extinction times. These mixtures also eschew sooty ignition (due to 
strong H2 presence), which can otherwise result in asymmetrically trapped soot that 
deteriorates flame sphericity. With respect to kinetic extinction, note that a step 
change from a higher flow rate to a lower one is needed because starting with a flow 
rate below the extinction limit would preclude flame establishment in the first place. 
The HIGHLY DESIRED experiment sets 3-4 utilize C 2H4 as fuel. With a nominal Le 
of unity with respect to air for this fuel, a baseline case (experiment set 3) for flame

stretch and thermaldiffusive stability effects is established. The fuel and inert mole 
fractions for the C 2H4/inert are varied to address different fuel concentration effects 
on sooting, which can impact Objectives ( A) flame spread behavior, ( B) extinction, 
and (C) flame stability. Soot will also enhance flame radiation. Since characteristic 
residence times will affect sooting tendenc ies, two flow rates are investigated for 
each mixture. Experiment set 4 replaces the inert, N 2, of set 3 with He, to better 
isolate Le>1 instabilities, corresponding to Objective ( C), as well as examine 
extinction for characteristically higher flame temperatures. 
The DESIRED experiment sets 5-6 examine the same fuel mixtures of the REQUIRED 
and HIGHLY DESIRED experiment sets, but with CO 2 as inert, including that for the 
ambient. N 2 and He are radiatively transparent gases; while CO 2 is an optically 
participating gas. While use of CO 2 should result in a characteristically lower flame 
temperature, the highly reabsorptive CO2 species can minimize net radiative heat loss 
affecting flame dynamics and extinction. Objectives ( A)-(C) are addressed by these 
experiments.

6. Success Criteria 
6.1. CLD Flame 
Success of the Coflow Laminar Diffusi on Flame experiment will be judged on 
meeting the stated experimental objectives by acquiring results that lead to the stated 
data end products. Three different levels of success – minimum, high, and complete 
success – are defined. An additional level of success is defined as satisfying our 
overall project goals, which is not required for complete experimental success. 
6.1.1. Minimum Success 
Minimum success is defined to mean acquis ition of sufficient scientific data from 
the experiment to perform a direct comp arison with the numerical computations 
and publish at least one journal article. This minimal level of success may be 
achieved by obtaining basic information about the flame characteristics from the 
color images or UV images, possibly for a subset of the flame conditions outlined 
above. Meaningful subsets of the data might include data from a single fuel 
(methane or ethylene, but not both) or from either weak or sooting flames, but not 
both. Data would remain valuable for comparisons with computational models, 
albeit not as complete as would be de sirable. For example, minimum success 
might come from obtaining data as follows: 
1. Color images of nonsooting flames only (SDEP A1). 
2. UV images of OH* luminosity from nonsooting flames (towards SDEP A2). 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science 
data end products including the following: 
- Observation of lift-off heights as a function of dilution level (SDEP A4). 
- Observation of extinction limits as a function of dilution level (SDEP A6). 
- Observation of flame shape and size (SDEP A5). 
- 2D images of OH* concentrations (SDEP A2). 
- Peak concentrations of OH* as a function of fuel dilution (SDEP A3). 
Similar “minimum success” subsets of data could be defined for sooting flames 
only, or datasets from one fuel only. In any of these cases, a paper could still be 
published on the limited results and their comparison to the computations. 
6.1.2. High Success 
High success is defined to mean acquisition of sufficient scientific data from the 
experiment to perform a direct comparis on with the numerical computations and 
publish several journal articles. In add ition to the information obtained for a 
minimum level of success, a high level of success may be achieved by obtaining 
more detailed information about the fl ame characteristics from UV images for 
species concentrations and from soot diagnostics for soot volume fraction (for 
example): 
1. 2D images of soot laser extinction and associated reference images 
2. 2D images of multi-color soot luminosity (from pyrometry data). 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science 
data end products including the following: 
- 2D images of soot volume fraction (SDEP B11).
