- 2D images of soot temperatures (SDEP B9). 
6.1.3. Complete Success 
Complete success is defined to mean acquisition of all data related to the 
experimental objectives. In addition to the information obtained for a high level 
of success, a complete level of succe ss may be achieved by obtaining complete 
information about the flame characteristics using the available diagnostic 
techniques, including full information on temperatures, extinction and sooting 
tendencies across the full range of flow conditions: 
1. Multi-color images of TFP data, including reference images. 
2. Images of soot extinction representing the peak soot volume fraction, including 
reference images. 
3. Soot luminosity images representing the peak soot temperature, including 
reference images. 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science 
data end products including the following: 
- Radial temperature profiles from TFP (SDEP A7 and B8). 
- Combined temperature fields from soot pyrometry and TFP (SDEP A7 and B8 
with B9). 
- Peak soot volume fraction as a function of fuel dilution over the full range of 
flow velocities (SDEP B12). 
- Peak temperature as a function of fu el dilution over the full range of flow 
velocities (SDEP A8 and B10).

Appendix A: Spherical Burner Design Reference 
 
Both the s-Flame and Flame Design research teams have significant experience with the 
manufacture of porous spherical burners from sintered metal. Both have relied upon an 
approach of fabricating the burners in lots and then testing them to identify the ones that best 
produce flames which are spherical and concentric with the burner. Given buoyancy’s role, this 
verification testing has been conducted in th e 2.2s Drop Tower or in normal gravity under 
conditions where buoyant effects have been reduced (but not eliminated). 
 
s-Flame 
 
The s-Flame burners are described in general te rms here, but note that a proprietary process 
was used for manufacturing the small burners. 
Sphere design: Sintered porous metal apparently works best, rather than porous ceramic or 
hollow spheres with holes created by EDM. The s pheres are "solid" with sintered grains except 
where the feed tube inserts. This was done by incorporating a feed tube during pressing/heating 
of the mold. This "tunnel" was then tapped for th e feed tube to be screwed into. The depth at 
which the feed tube is inserted into the 'tunnel' is a key parameter, as there is a small volume, or 
open cavity, at the 'center' of the burner, that a ffects flow uniformity. The depth of the feed tube 
penetration was optimized via modeling with CFD. If it is possible to pr ess the mold uniformly 
(radially), rather than in 2 hemispheres (as done by the company), that should work best. 
Sphere material:- sintered bronze (and possibly other materials) 
Sphere sizes: at least 1/8” to ½” in diameter. Commercially, >1/2" diameters work best. 
Smaller sizes need to be manufactured at Princeton to work well. 
Sphere manufacturer: Custom-fabricated spheres from Princeton are believed to give the best 
results. GKN Sintered Metals has manufactured the spheres with a provided spec and protocol. 
Tube diameter: These sizes of the feed tubes depende d on the burner sizes. For the 1/4" and 
1/2" diameter porous burners, the tubi ng used are 0.025" O.D./0.017" I.D. and 0.058" 
O.D./0.042" I.D., respectively. 
Tube attachment: The feed tubes are threaded, and the spheres are tapped, to establish the 
supply connection. There is no sealant used for th e threaded joints. Since the tube is inserted 
almost to the center, s-Flame rarely has leaking effects. 
Burner verification: Flame shape for inverse diffusion flames in a micro-buoyancy chamber is 
the standard test for s-Flame. There is a bi g difference between diffusion flames and premixed 
flames, as the issuing velocity is at least an order of magnitude less for the diffusion flames. 
Successful fabrication: For the commercial spheres, perhaps 30% are acceptable. Sometimes, 
only 1 in 10 work out. 
Thermocouple attachment: The s-Flame researchers measure the burner surface temperature

the standard test for s-Flame. There is a bi g difference between diffusion flames and premixed

Heat Flux Gages 
The recommended Medtherm sensors are from their 64 Series: Heat Flux Transducers and 
Infrared Radiometers for the Direct Measurement of Heat Transfer Rates. The PI team uses the 
Schmidt-Boelter gage with a multi-junction thermop ile. This is important because of the goal 
that the sensor surface have a uniform temperatur e (in contrast to the alternative Gardon gage). 
A thermocouple also measures the temperature of the sensor. There is no transmitting window 
or aperture. The Medtherm thermopile gage has a nominal absorptance of 0.95 over a spectral 
range of 0.6 to 15.0 µm. Currently, the PI team uses 10 mV output at a full range of 100 kW/m 2. 
Recent drop tests indicate an in itial heat flux of about 50 kW/m 2 at ignition and then generally 
dropping to values of about 5 kW/m 2. As the Medtherm sensors can easily over range by 150%, 
within their linear calibration, the 10 mV lim it can be exceeded. The sensors have reported 
maximum non-linearity of 2 % of full range and a repeatability of 0.5 %. They are calibrated 
with an uncertainty of 3 %. The sensor has a respons e time of less than 250 ms. For ground-
based operation water-cooling is important, but circulating water is not needed during 
spaceflight. Tests by the PI team have shown that water condensation and sensor overheating 
are unlikely for the proposed flight test matrix. The sensor thermocouple specification is 
sufficient for operation without water, provid ed the sensor does not exceed 600 ºF (316 ºC), 
which is the maximum (body) temperature for the Space Shuttle Flight Qualified sensors.

Surface Temperature Measurement 
The temperature of the outlet plate should be me asured as the burner surface temperature. To 
represent its distribution throughout the area, the thermocouples should be placed at two 
positions, close to or corresponding to where the heat flux sensors are located. In the early 
ground experiments, two K-type 0.01”diameter bare wire thermocouples were used, sewed into 
the screen. Thermocouples thermally bonded to th e outlet plate are needed for the spaceflight 
experiment.

8.0 Output FILES 
8.1 Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc. 
The file contains a two-line header. The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a 
SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains. The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data. The 
text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on 
whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column headings should match the data 
which is the following: 
- A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. 
- 25 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-225 board in the order shown in Table 2. (The names of 
many of these values change depending on whether it is a BRE test or not, hence the two options for header.) 
- Channel AO-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board. This is the E-Field control voltage. 
Rows of comma-separated data is added to the file between DataRecordingStart and DataRecordingStop commands at a 
rate defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Error! Reference source not found., defaulting to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling.

3 
 
8.2 Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY 
is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes. The date in the name is when the log file is 
created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category. The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MM-
DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory. See 
section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if 
desired. 
8.3 Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters. Command log 
files contain only the details of each command received. The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-
DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log. The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the 
command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including 
header information.

Science Summary 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under 
development with a set of four independent experiments which are each focused on 
advancing combustion technology through fundamental research. The current ACME 
experiments are specifically directed at addressing energy and environmental concerns. 
The overall goals are to improve our understanding of (1) combustion at fuel lean 
conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, (2) 
combustion of fuels with increased hydrogen content which could enable reduced 
greenhouse emission, (3) soot control and reduction, (4) oxygen enriched combustion 
which could enable practical carbon sequestration, and (5) use of electric fields for 
combustion control. Unlike the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX), ACME is not 
focused on the advancement of spacecraft fire safety technology, although it is likely 
that some ACME findings will be relevant. While distinct, the experiments share several 
significant traits. The principal unifying feature of the ACME experiments is their use of 
gaseous fuels (e.g., methane and ethylene) rather than liquid or solid fuels. With this in 
common, the experiments will be conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) through the use of a single modular insert. In addition to the fuel state, the current 
set of ACME experiments all use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., diffusion) flames for their 
studies. To simplify analysis, these flames are either one or two dimensional, 
depending upon the experiment. 
 
A general goal of the current ACME experiments is to gain fundamental understanding 
that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion 
processes, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical 
kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations. In addition to enhanced 
performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost 
for combustor design. In summary, microgravity investigations of non-premixed flames 
could lead to eco-friendly combustion systems providing our nation with green power for 
the future. 
 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) 
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that 
our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel 
dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. 
The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to 
extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and 
experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels. The 
dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be

ty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. 
The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to 
extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and 
experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels. The 
dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be 
carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions.

Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in 
an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be directly 
applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame 
stability, and more. 
 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present 
as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion 
wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat 
transfer, and reduce pollutant emission. The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is to gain an improved 
understanding of flame ion production and investigate how the ions can be used to 
control non-premixed flames. Outside reviewers concluded that the experiment “… will 
contribute to our critical understanding to our knowledge of combustion processes in the 
presence of electric fields.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas-jet 
flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) 
differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the 
burner. Measurements, as a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will be made of 
the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
Flame Design 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of 
soot inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched 
combustion and the “design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free. 
An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved 
burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design 
will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, 
created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment. Tests will be conducted 
with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and oxygen in 
order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception. The effect of 
the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both normal flames 
and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from the 
spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere. The Flame Design experiment will 
explore whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and 
flammability limits for non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an 
indicator of those limits for premixed flames.

Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) 
The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment 
is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of 
both soot-free and sooty flames. The spherical flame, which is only possible in 
microgravity, will be created through use of a porous spherical burner from which a 
fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the CIR chamber. Flames will be ignited at non-
steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally toward extinction. Tests will be 
conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere. The 
fuel gases include hydrogen and methane for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty 
flames. One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative 
and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, 
respectively). Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of 
pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with 
fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The ACME project currently includes four distinct experiments and will tentatively include 
even more in the future. Therefore, it is critical that the project adopt a flexible approach 
to experiment control. This flexibility can be achieved through a set of explicit, and 
generally predefined and verified, functions which can be selected, repeated as needed, 
and ordered to create a variety of overall experiment sequences. Functions can include 
variable parameters, e.g., flow rate(s), providing additional flexibility. Furthermore, 
experiments can be run via either operator or software control. This approach to 
operational (ops) control is similar to the ordered stringing of beads to make a necklace, 
where each bead represents a function, and where each bead’s characteristics (e.g., 
color, shape, size) represent its function and the associated variable parameters. The 
approach is further explained in section 1 of this document, i.e., General Requirements. 
 
As defined herein, the control functions almost always occur in a serial fashion, but 
multiple operations may occur simultaneously. For example, sequential functions may 
in turn activate non-imaging and imaging data acquisition, the CIR illumination package, 
and fuel flow such that all are active at the same time. While these are operating, a 
timed function can also occur, e.g., translating the TFP fiber array. Normally, only a 
single timed function will be operative at a time, given their serial arrangement. 
However, there is at least one critical exception, namely the automated detection of 
extinction, where that function should normally always be active following ignition when

1. [CIR & ACME] General Requirements 
1.1. [general] ACME shall provide flexible experiment control based on explicit 
functions which can be selected, repeated as needed, and ordered ( like colored 
beads on a string) to create a variety of overall experiment sequences. Where 
possible, flexibility shall be provided within the individual functions by allowing 
the specification of relevant parameters ( like the flow rate, or by analog the size 
of the bead). Flexibility is critical for avoiding limitations that could hinder 
operations or limit ACME science. For example, the SOFBALL experiment 
(STS-83, STS-94, and STS -107) initially had a hard shutoff at 5 minutes 
because it was fully expected that the flames would extinguish by that time. 
However, that assumption was found to be faulty and the tests terminated while 
flames were still burning diminishing the scientific return. The test duration could 
not be extended until a subsequent spaceflight . Flexible experiment control will 
also enable future ACME experiments which differ operationally from the current 
set of ACME experiments. 
1.2. [general] During at least combustion, ACME shall be capable of operations by 
either automated software control or operator control. ACME shall furthermore 
be capable of both automated and operat or control within a single test, but 
where automated and operator control are not required simultaneously. 
Software control allows for a higher fidelity of time control (e.g., as can be 
important for some experiments or tests), while operator control allows a human 
response to downlinked measurements, which can be especially valuable when 
trying to either identify or test at (or near) limit conditions, e.g., for soot inception, 
lifting, or extinction. 
1.3. [general] ACME shall provide for automated software control through sequences 
of functions that are each either instant (i.e., without a duration) or timed, i.e., 
with a variable duration that is a parameter of that function.

developing and using new operational functions, for ISS operations after the

experiment may have several different operational sequences, and at least one

The provided examples are quite similar, especially in the pre-ignition and post-

are certainly possible in any section of the operations. 
 
 
 
Appendix A: Variation Examples 
This section provides depictions of major ways in which the three ACME gas flows, TFP 
array position, and electric field potential can be varied. Note that the TFP array cannot 
be moved instantaneously so the stepped and rectangular wave functions are not 
applicable. And while relatively abrupt changes in flow are possible (at least in the gas-
jet burners), it should be understood that the control will not be accurate during rapid 
transitions because of the limited response time of the Mass Flow Controllers. Finally, 
note that while time durations are generally shown as either 0 or 10 seconds in the 
presented examples, this was done as a convenience and the functions allow for 
durations of varying values. Finally, it should be emphasized that these are just 
examples, where a careful review of the function requirements will reveal additional 
details.

Operational Sequence for Flame Design Spherical Flame Tests 
 
Action 
Approx. 
Time 
1. Ensure that 6.4 mm spherical burner is installed. Preflow the burner fluent g as 
at the composition of the upcoming test point to flush the plumbing system. 
2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point pressure and 
species compositions, as specified in the test matrix. Conditions are obtained in 
four ways: from cabi n air (desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and 
replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge. 
3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of 5 minutes is 
required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed conditions. 
4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for video 
cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring measurements. After 15 s, 
commence fluent flow, ignite flame, and retract ignitor. 
Perform either Steps 5, 6, and 8 OR Steps 7 and 8. 
5. Soot inception limit. Allow the flame to pass its soot -inception limit. 
Continuously record temperature distributions. 
6. Radiative extinction. Detect radiative extinction with a PMT or with near real -
time video. Continuously record temperature distr ibutions. At uplinkable time 
(estimated 3 s) after extinction, reduce flow rate by uplinkable amount (estimated 
50%) for uplinkable time (estimated 5 s) to confirm extinction. If the flame 
reappears, return to the initial flow rate and return to the beginning of Step 6. 
Otherwise terminate the fluent flow. 
7. Kinetic extinction. After an uplinkable time (estimated 10 s), decrease fluent 
flow rate linearly in time such that flow rate becomes zero at uplinkable time 
(estimated 30 s) after ignition. Detect kinetic extinction with a PMT or with near 
real-time video. Continuously record temperature distributions. At uplinkable time 
(estimated 3 s) after extinction detection, increase flow rate by uplinkable amount 
(estimated 100%) for uplinkable time (estimated 5 s) to confirm extinction. If the 
flame reappears, return to the initial flow rate and return to the beginning of Step 7. 
Otherwise terminate the fluent flow. 
8. Record reference images (if applicable). After 60 s terminate color imaging and 
monitoring measurements. Select data for downlink and downlink data.

1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s BRE experiment to facilitate its 
analysis. The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of soot or the 
combustion gases. For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-imaging 
measurements. Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational 
logs provide information that can support the analysis. 
 
It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the BRE data begin by familiarizing themselves 
with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the BRE Final Report or the more 
comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. 
 
Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document. To interpret the non-imaging data, 
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 19039A1_data.csv, which has 
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The data 
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface 
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D).

addressed in ACME-RPT-011. 
 
 
2. BRE Overview 
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/BRE Final Report, which also provides descriptions of the 
science, preliminary results, and more. It is strongly suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in 
analyzing the BRE data. 
 
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within 
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G. Quintiere of the Department of Fire 
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), 
namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global, 
retired). The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student 
in the Fire Protection Engineering department. 
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64. 
More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Feb. to April 2019, while the second-
round testing occurred from Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021. The first round of tests was limited to ethylene and 
the 25-mm BRE burner, while the second round also included tests with methane and the 50-mm burner 
(although not together).

were conducted on April 5. Nonetheless, the BRE (and more generally ACME) test days and numbers are 
identified by the date on which the test day began, even if they occurred after midnight (whether on the

The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 45 
flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, when an 
additional 17 flames were ignited. BRE’s second-round flame testing began in Sept. 2020, during 
Increment 63, in which 47 flames were ignited. The second and final round of tests was 
completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames were ignited. As a result, 
62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and second rounds of testing for a total 
of 194 flames. 
 
The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI 
team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests 
to maximize its scientific outcome. However, the break was longer than had been planned 
because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew availability. As a result, BRE’s 
second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds of the preceding ACME experiment, 
Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), was completed, where that 
occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was the delayed start of commercial crew 
launches and understanding that crew availability would be limited until such crew launches 
entered an operational, rather than demonstration, phase. 
 
All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene 
(C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range of chamber 
pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in 
future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric 
conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. 
In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any combustion products (e.g., water 
vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the 
chamber atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But during tests 
days, the atmosphere was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests. 
Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and 50 mm, 
and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen. Therefore, the 
second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than investigated during the first 
round. However, in contrast to the first round most of the round 2 tests were carried out at 
roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary effect on flames.

BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are independently 
conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple 
hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) is the primary 
component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-
carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting because of its carbon

1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D). The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number). As such, the example, 19039A1 is test A1 conducted 
on the 39th day of 2019. But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 40th) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 19039B1, 19039B2, and 19039B3) are 
typically similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or 
repeat. Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0. While initially used 
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a related 
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all. The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted 
alphabetically. However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins 
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter. 
 
The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by 
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The first row is a header and provides a limited

B. Image Files 
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: 
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera 
ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
 High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
 
The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used 
for BRE or most of the current ACME experiments. Of the ACME investigations, the LLL-UV camera 
was only used by the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) study. 
 
1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera 
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera. Its primary 
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is 
also often referred to as the operations or ops camera. 
 
The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera 
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps. It is not recorded on the space station 
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/. That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.

Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often 
downlinked during a test day. Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon 
object (HOBJ) format, which is not readily opened with typical image processing software. 
The image data was made available in that raw format and later in a converted TIFF format, 
where the NASA conversion was carried out without each of the following: 
• color balancing (to avoid possible saturation as subsequently discussed) 
• dark frame subtraction 
• removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage) 
Furthermore, the NASA conversion employs a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is 
detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) as it 
will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers. The priority in the NASA conversion

To use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements, it is critical to avoid saturation, 
for example by using a camera gain of zero. Another employed approach was to not use the 
camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and 1.68, 
respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation. Such multiplication can be 
done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the white 
balancing is accomplished with the commands: 
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68 
clip 4095 
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software 
because the color balancing was at least generally not done with the hardware to avoid the 
risk of saturation. 
 
However, in carrying out color-ratio pyrometry calculations for the ISS data from ACME’s CLD 
Flame experiment, the investigators determined that the three color ratios (e.g., blue/red) 
didn’t result in the same temperature profile until the green channel was adjusted by 10%. 
This notably differs from the camera’s default of multiplication by 1 (i.e., no multiplication) 
for the green color plane.

Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format 
with 12-bit image data. As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be 
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced. Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021 
 
15 
 
 
susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit. As a result, the images feature hot pixels which 
increase in number over the months and years in space. As such, it will appear as if there is a 
star field within the combustion chamber. Therefore, the images should ideally be processed 
to remove the bright outlying hot spots. Radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera 
imaging. 
 
Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure 
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames. As a 
result, the framing rate was typically far less. Different exposures are often selected for 
different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate 
may not be consistent. Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating 
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under 
uncertain or varying flame intensities. Bracketing can also used to simultaneously accomplish 
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP 
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame. 
 
In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file 
which should be available for each successful flame test, e.g., to verify the exposure duration. 
These files are in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet 
software or alternately as a text file. Column headings are found in the first row of such files.

Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright 
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward. In 
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s 
long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis. This is contrary to an ACME 
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis 
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format. In this regard, the science requirements were not 
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs. 
 
There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely 
reproducible. Therefore, the scaling of the image data should ideally be established for each 
subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a test day. The scaling can 
typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin Filament 
Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions. 
Meanwhile, the other cameras used in ACME testing had fixed lenses.

4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR’s 
collimated illumination package. The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet 
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter, but it may also be useful for 
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction. However, the camera’s red filter, 
corresponding to the red illumination, appears to be broad enough to permit significant soot 
incandescence to pass through the filter. As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for 
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions. After post-processing on the ground, 
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened. The 
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps. 
 
It is important to understand that this camera’s images are of limited value for BRE because 
of the general lack of soot with exception of ignition. But even considering that, the soot 
volume fraction can be computed using images from the ACME DataCam as discussed in that 
camera’s section. 
 
In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, this 
monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera 
is nearly insensitive to blue. The red filter was installed on 5 March 2018 and used throughout 
all subsequent ACME testing.

1. CIR chamber calculator file 
In great contrast to other file types, there is just a single file for each of BRE’s two rounds of 
testing: 
 Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2019-01-31 to 2019-04-09.xlsx 
 Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2020-07-22 to 2021-02-03.xlsx 
which provide estimates of the composition of the combustion chamber before and after each 
BRE test, and more generally for every Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) action 
involving gas flow into or out of the chamber. As a result, this includes filling and venting 
operations, plus recirculation of the chamber contents through the adsorber cartridge filled 
with 13x molecular sieves. 
 
More specifically, the chamber calculator provides the chamber pressure before and after 
each operation involving flow into or out of the chamber. While the standard ACME data 
output files (discussed in section 4.A.1) provide the chamber pressure throughout each test,

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021 
 
20 
 
 
that measurement is from a pressure transducer that hasn’t been calibrated in years. 
Meanwhile, the calibrations of the corresponding CIR pressure transducers are checked every 
six months and those calibrations are updated if needed. Therefore, the chamber calculator 
is the more reliable source of the chamber pressure. 
 
The pressure in the CIR chamber is measured by four different CIR pressure transducers, of 
which one (PT29) is a different model used for safety. The output of the other three 
transducers were used to obtain an average chamber pressure. However, the output of one 
of those (PT28) was clearly an outlier from the other two (PT16 and PT17) as well that of PT29. 
Therefore, the average pressure recorded in the chamber calculator file was later based on 
just PT16 and PT17. 
 
For BRE, the chamber calculator also provides concentration estimates of the following gases 
within the chamber before and after each test and FOMA operation: 
Oxygen & nitrogen: O2, N2 
Fuels: CH4, C2H4 
Combustion products: CO2, H2O 
The latter are based on telemetry from the three Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) on the ACME 
chamber insert for the flow of fuel, oxygen (or inert), and nitrogen. 
 
In a test, the chamber calculator assumes either complete combustion or no combustion, 
where in the former case the reactant flowing from the burner is transformed into carbon 
dioxide and water vapor (or water vapor alone if the fuel was hydrogen). Failed or 
unsustained ignitions were typically set to assume no ignition. Short-lived flames were often 
treated as having complete combustion, even if a significant fraction of the reactant didn’t 
burn. However, adjustments can be made to account for partial combustion by appropriate 
selection of the ‘Burn Fraction’ in column AL. 
 
With recirculation of the chamber contents, the calculator assumes that the carbon dioxide 
and water vapor are completely adsorbed, i.e., removed from the chamber. Meanwhile, it 
assumes that any unburnt fuels are not adsorbed. 
 
Researchers can of course make their estimates of the chamber contents where the chamber 
calculator should nonetheless be referenced for its record of fills, venting, and recirculation. 
Note that the chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed 
hardware. Unfortunately, it is not yet possible to compare chamber calculator estimates with 
measurements that were sometimes made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentation Package (GCIP). Concentrations from the latter are not yet available as 
explained in section 4.A.3 of this document.

3. Notes 
Notes of various types are available for test days, where not all types were collected or 
necessarily prepared for each test day. It is important to understand that the notes, whether 
handwritten or typed, may include mistakes. It is better to rely on automated logs, metadata 
files, and parameter files or of course the measurements themselves when possible. 
 
The daily test point logs, with names such as ‘19039 daily test point log.pdf,’ chronologically 
list the tests and the image data acquired which was to be downlinked. Typically, image data 
was not downlinked without successful, i.e., sustained, ignition. As an example, image data 
wasn’t downlinked if the test aborted prior to ignition. However, the reverse is not always 
true. Image data was sometimes downlinked when ignition was unsuccessful and as a result 
the test point log is only a clue as to what transpired. Furthermore, note that image data 
from certain selected cameras, e.g., the HiBMs camera, was sometimes not downlinked due 
to the limit of how much data could be reasonably downlinked in a subsequent two-shift day. 
 
Notes with names such as ‘19039 flow traces.pdf’ include preliminary plots of the flow rates 
(as seen on a console during testing) and other flame diagnostics, typically along with 
additional information about the tests. 
 
The test parameter notes, with names such as ‘19039 test parameter notes.pdf,’ show the 
parameter values which were planned in advance of the test day and the changes made 
during the test day. 
 
The test sheets, with names such as ‘19039 test sheets.pdf,’ are summary notes about the 
conduct of each tests conducted that day.

Relationship to NASA Flammability 
Tests 1 and 2 
• The Upward Flame Propagation (Test 1) is the dominant 
test for material flammability by NASA. 
 
– It tests the flame propagation of a vertical sample 30 × 6.4 – 
7.5 cm wide, under a small electric source heat flux of 75 
kW/m2. 
– The atmospheric conditions are controlled. 
– Burn length and time are recorded. 
– It is considered a pass-fail type test. 
 
• The NASA Test 2: Cone Calorimeter with external heat 
fluxes of 25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement information gained 
from Test 1.

2. Background Microgravity 
Studies 
10

11 
Background of Combustion in 
Microgravity 
• Experiments in Skylab (Ross, 2001; Kimzey, 1974) indicated sustained 
burning of thin paper and plastics. 
• More recent experiments indicate flame spread on thin paper and plastic 
thin cylinders in microgravity (Ross, 2001). 
• Opposed flow spread in a quiescent atmosphere has been shown to 
depend on material, thickness, and oxygen concentration (Ross, 2001). 
• The burning of candle flames on the MIR (Ross, 2001) last for periods 
ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A spherical flame 
formed around the wick. 
• Droplet experiments by Kumagai and others (Ross, 2001). 
• Small diameter jet flames of 0.4 – 2.7 mm yielded spherical flames of 
durations from 150 – 300 s (Ross, 2001). 
• Sunderland et al. (1999) recorded flames for port diameters up to 3.3 mm, 
and Re from about 10 – 1700 in microgravity. 
• Brahmi et al. (2005) used a gaseous burner to simulate burning in g. They 
burned ethane over a 60  60 mm sintered bronze plate in O2-N2 flowing 
at velocities of 10 – 150 mm/s. 
• Bustamante (2012) aircraft and drop data on flat liquid-fueled wicks.

Knowledge Lacking and Knowledge 
to be Gained by Flight Tests 
• The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the 
range of steady burning conditions for condensed fuels 
in microgravity. We will identify the associated material 
properties and the real materials that are represented. 
 
• Once established based on fuel properties, NASA Test 2 
could be used as a basis for establishing comparable 
properties for real materials. This could elevate the role 
of NASA Test 2 over Test 1. This would close the loop of 
using a ground-based test to assess the true 
flammability of materials in microgravity.

Science Data End Products 
38 
Objective 
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity 
for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular 
burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 
ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 
concentrations and pressures. Emphasize conditions that 
can be related to diverse condensed fuels. 
 
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of 
O2/CO2 (desired). 
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction 
limits.

Justification for Extended-
Duration Microgravity 
• The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft 
owing to considerable g-jitter disturbances. 
 
• Testing in NASA 5.2-s drop facility indicated possible approach to 
steady burning. 
 
• The longer duration testing in the ISS will facilitate the efficient 
operation of the BRE to exploit a relatively quick record of results 
over a range of flow rates. This will insure a complete 
flammability map in microgravity.

6. Operational Sequence 
67

BRE Operational Sequence 
 Action Approx. 
Time 
1. Ensure that the appropriate burner is installed. Preflow the 
burner fluent gas at the composition of the upcoming test point 
to flush the plumbing system. 
2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point 
pressure and species compositions, as specified in the test 
matrix. Conditions are obtained in four ways: from cabin air 
(desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and 
replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge. 
3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of 
5 minutes is required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed 
conditions. 
4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for 
video cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring 
measurements and wait 15 s. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
68

BRE Operational Sequence 
 Action Approx. 
Time 
5. Commence fluent flow at a value to be uplinked. The initial 
value should correspond to about 1 g/m2-s of hydrocarbon fuel. 
Energize igniter to ignite the flame and then retract the igniter. 
If ignition does not occur within 5 seconds, shut off the flow. A 
new value of flow rate will be specified by uplink. If the flame 
ignites, proceed to Step 6. Otherwise proceed to Step 7. 
6. Set the flow rate to the test flow rate. Anytime during this step, 
if the flame extinguishes, or either heat flux sensor exceeds a 
critical temperature, stop the fuel flow. Continue until the 
surface burner temperatures become quasi-steady. Then 
reduce the flow rate in 10% increments of the test flow rate, 
hold for 15 s, and continue such reductions until extinction. 
7. Stop fluent flow. Record reference images (if applicable). After 
60 s terminate color imaging and monitoring measurements. 
Select data for downlink and downlink data.

Heat flux measurement 
• The incident heat flux is conductive and radiative. 
• Heat flux gages in the surface will record incident 
heat flux. 
• Thermocouples in the surface will record the Ts 
distribution. 
• Surface reradiative flux scales with Ts 4. 
• Flow rate will be varied to obtain a wide range of L.

6 
Motivation 
• Many condensed fuels have a critical heat flux (CHF) 
below which ignition and spread is impossible. 
 
• This CHF depends on the surface heat loss rate. 
 
• Buoyant cooling occurs in 1g, so CHF is lower in g. 
 
• BRE will identify g CHF for condensed fuels. 
 
Condensed fuel ignition in g will generally be easier 
than on Earth.

7 
NASA Test 1 
• The Upward Flame Propagation 
(Test 1) is NASA’s main test for 
material flammability in 
spacecraft. 
• It tests the flame propagation of a 
vertical sample 30  6.4 – 7.5 cm. 
• Burn length (15 cm threshold) and 
time are recorded. 
• It is a pass-fail test. 
• It is similar to UL-94, whose 
performance scales with hc / L .

8 
NASA Test 2 
• Ohlemiller (1992) found that NASA Test 1 results did not 
correlate with NIST flammability tests of ignition, burning 
rate, and opposed flow flame spread. 
• He recommended that Test 1 be modified to include the 
addition of external radiant heating. 
• NASA Test 2 uses a cone calorimeter with heat fluxes of 
25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement Test 1. 
• Tests 1 and 2 do not explicitly predict performance in g. 
Ohlemiller recommended g tests, 
stating “Without such information 
spacecraft designers are confronted 
with unquantifiable risks regarding 
fire safety.”

9 
Relating material properties to g flammability 
Can 1g properties be related to g flammability? 
 
• This works for to UL-94 in 1g, whose performance 
scales with hc / L . 
• If it works in g, a limited number of g tests could 
be used to predict ignition, burning, and extinction 
behavior of many materials. 
 
A BRE goal is to furnish g measurements relating 
ignition, burning, and extinction to material properties 
that are obtainable in 1g.

10 
g combustion surprises 
• Quasisteady burning of condensed fuels in g has 
rarely been observed. 
• Several surprises were seen in tests of g droplets 
and flame spread, including those associated with 
3D effects, flaming fire brands, radiative extinction, 
etc. 
• The effects of radiative feedback have not been 
explored.

11 
The MIR fire 
• In the MIR fire a solid propellant oxygen generator 
ignited, producing a 1 m flame. 
• If this flame had impinged on other materials, could 
they have burned self-sustained? 
• Material flammability in space must be better 
understood.

12 
Past condensed fuel combustion in g 
• Experiments in Skylab indicated sustained burning 
of thin paper and plastics. 
• Spread on 4.5 mm diameter rods of Delrin, PMMA 
and HDPE was achieved in opposed flows down to 
1 cm/s. 
• Opposed flow spread in quiescent g depends on 
material, thickness, and oxygen concentration. 
• Droplet flames of Kumagai, Williams, and co-
workers.

13 
Candles in g 
• Candle flames on MIR survived from 1 – 45 
min. Hemispherical flames were observed. 
• Dietrich and T’ien’s glovebox tests had 
much shorter durations. 
• The MIR flights had XO2 = 0.22 – 0.25 and a 
metal screen enclosure. 
• The glovebox had XO2 = 0.217 and a 
perforated plastic enclosure. 
Sustained burning of condensed fuels in g without 
external radiation is confirmed.

14 
Flame shape in g 
• Sunderland and co-workers found g gas jet flames 
to be spherical at low Re, and longer than 1g 
flames. 
• Candle and droplet flames also are spherical in g. 
• Planar surfaces in g can produce spherical flames.

15 
• Torero and co-workers 
burned ethane in a 60  60 
mm porous burner in g. 
• Oxidizer flow rates were 10 
– 150 mm/s. 
• Three flame shape regimes 
were observed: elliptical (I); 
parabolic (II); and flat (III). 
• BRE is likely to encounter 
all 3 shapes.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
The goal of this research is to establish the burning conditions possible in a microgravity 
quiescent environment. The approach is to do this using a burner to emulate (BRE, Burning Rate 
Emulator) the burning for real condensed fuels, representative of common liquids and solids. 
This will be done for steady burning conditions, albeit ideal in some cases, but the BRE will 
range over a wide spectrum of real fuel properties. The key properties governing steady burning 
are (1) the heat of gasification, (2) the surface reradiation heat flux, and (3) the heat of 
combustion. Flame radiation is also relevant in general and can be represented in terms of the 
laminar smoke point. Its importance in microgravity flames needs study, but the first three 
properties are key. 
 Currently NASA assesses the flammability hazard of materials for use in space flight by 
an upward flame spread “pass-fail” test (Test 1), and supplements with data from the Cone 
Calorimeter (Test 2). The latter test has the capability of measuring the three properties listed 
above. Hence, the successful application of the BRE in microgravity can enhance the usefulness 
of Test 2. 
 Fundamental and ad hoc testing in microgravity at quiescent conditions has shown that 
steady flames can be supported on candle wicks, droplets, jets and, at very low ambient 
velocities, small plastic samples and a burner flame. The established flames tend to have 
spherical or semi-ellipsoidal shapes. Our preliminary work burning ethanol on planar wicks of 1 
× 4 cm suggest similar shapes in aircraft and drop tower tests. But this work showed instabilities 
in the drop tower, and needs further exploration. Theoretical analysis based on microgravity jet 
flame length correlations suggests that a 50 mm diameter planar material could support steady 
combustion in microgravity for some liquid and plastic fuels. The analysis indicates that burning 
depends on diameter, so several additional burner sizes will be needed to examine this effect. 
 Gas burners like the BRE have been used to successfully simulate burning of a wide 
range of fuels in terms of their B numbers and configurations over a range of Grashof numbers. 
We have successfully shown that for planar burning at different angle orientations that a burner 
can emulate the flame standoff distribution, and even match the onset of unsteadiness to 
turbulent flow. Theoretical analyses of such a problem are limited by the inability to accurately 
deal with flame radiation, turbulence and variable properties. A burner simulation can be far 
superior as it inherently contains these effects. 
 The construction of a 50 mm diameter prototype BRE burner with flame heat flux sensors 
has enabled us to emulate both a methanol and heptane pool fire of the 50 mm diameter, 
reproducing its color, flame character and shape, and heat of gasification for nearly the same 
surface temperatures.

1. INTRODUCTION 
1.1 Goal of the study 
The goal of this study is to establish the burning conditions for materials in a quiescent 
microgravity environment. The burning conditions will represent those of steady burning with 
the heat of gasification of the material as the principal fuel property that controls such burning. 
In addition, the heat of combustion controlling flame extent, surface reradiation heat flux, and 
flame radiation properties will influence the burning rate. We seek to define the burning in terms 
of these properties by using an emulator having a controlled gaseous fuel supply to simulate 
steady burning of material with those properties. The burning rate emulator (BRE) can be 
operated to represent a range of real solid and liquid fuels, and considering an effective heat of 
gasification can also simulate an applied external heat flux.

aterial properties 
On Earth, gravity assists flow in fire to supply air and promote fire spread. For many solid and 
some common liquid fuels, preheating is needed to achieve burning. Materials have a critical 
heat flux (CHF) below which ignition is not possible. This CHF depends on the heat loss from 
the material on heating, and convective heat loss contributes. The convective loss is purely 
diffusive in microgravity, and therefore the CHF is lower. So ignition of materials in spacecraft 
under microgravity conditions could be somewhat easier than on Earth in a quiescent atmosphere. 
For comfort in a spacecraft environment there is likely to be some small ambient flow with 
velocities of about 6 – 20 cm/s (Ross, 2001). Such flows are known to promote spread and

4 
burning in microgravity. But it is useful to examine, in the extreme, the conditions of burning in 
a purely quiescent atmosphere. Results in quiescent conditions certainly set a floor for the 
burning conditions. For fire safety in space it is important to know the burning conditions of a 
given fuel. Currently there is no way to determine these conditions. The present study seeks to 
express these conditions in terms of measureable material properties, and to consider the role of 
external heat addition, so important to fire growth on Earth. 
Current flammability criteria for space flight applications are contained in documents PSS-
01-721 and NHB 8060-1 (1998) as prescribed, respectively, by ESA and NASA. The documents 
are considered as equivalent. The Upward Flame Propagation (Test 1) is the dominant test for 
material flammability by NASA. It tests the flame propagation of a vertical sample 30 × 6.4 – 
7.5 cm wide, under a small electric source heat flux of 75 kW/m 2. The atmospheric conditions 
are controlled. Burn length and time are recorded. It is considered a pass-fail type test, similar to 
the UL-94 test, commonly used by industry for plastic components. The latter uses a premixed 
flame source, and samples 12.5 × 1.3 cm. In UL-94 the pass-fail performance could be correlated 
with the ratio of the heat of combustion to heat of gasification for a material (Downey, 2009). 
Ohlemiller (1992) found that NASA Test 1 results for a material did not correlate with 
NIST flammability tests that measure ignition, burning rate, and opposed flow flame spread. He 
recommended that Test 1 be modified to include the addition of external radiant heating. In fact, 
the current NASA requirements use the Cone Calorimeter with external heat fluxes of 25 – 
75 kW/m 2 (Test 2) to supplement information gained from Test 1. Test 1 with a “pass-fail” 
criteria, and even supplemental information gained from Test 2, do not explicitly give a basis for 
predicting performance in microgravity. Indeed, Ohlemiller recommended the study of flame 
spread in microgravity using a prescribed flow and heat flux. He said, “Without such information, 
spacecraft designers are confronted with unquantifiable risks regarding fire safety.” The FIST 
program with Fernandez-Pello at UC Berkeley (Ross, 2001) is the only current program aimed to 
examine these combined effects of radiation and flow. Nevertheless, the current NASA material 
compliance by flammability testing does not give information needed to predict performance in 
microgravity. 
There is a need to establish a basis for testing flammability on Earth to extrapolate to 
microgravity applications. First, there is a need to establish the conditions of burning in 
microgravity. Secondly, it is essential to represent the condition of burning in terms of 
established models and material properties. The correlation of performance in UL-94 with the

There is a need to establish a basis for testing flammability on Earth to extrapolate to 
microgravity applications. First, there is a need to establish the conditions of burning in 
microgravity. Secondly, it is essential to represent the condition of burning in terms of 
established models and material properties. The correlation of performance in UL-94 with the 
property ratio, heat of combustion to heat of gasification, shows a linkage to the NASA Test 1 
test. Both of these properties are determinable from the NASA Test 2 test, as demonstrated by 
Tewarson (2002). Thirdly, as steady burning is directly related to the heat of gasification 
property, the establishment of quiescent burning in microgravity would provide a direct 
connection between a property and burning. Truly, some materials, such as those that char, do 
not fit this simple steady burning model, yet their burning character can still be approximately 
represented by a relatively high heat of gasification. For example, while wood burns unsteadily 
with a char, its average burning rate can be represented by an effective heat of gasification of 4 – 
6 kJ/g. Fourthly, a burning rate emulator (BRE) can potentially display the conditions of burning 
in microgravity experiments. Hence the BRE can be used to assess a range of burning conditions 
to find a domain of burning and the properties that would allow it. Moreover, the simple burning 
model indicated by Eqs. (1) – (3) would allow the prediction of burning with the addition of 
radiant heat flux. While we do not intend to vary the external heat flux, the results of the BRE 
can be interpreted in terms of these relationships. The BRE can determine a range of burning

5 
conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied 
radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. The latter two properties can be varied by 
changing the gaseous fuel supply of the BRE. In addition, nitrogen can be added to the gaseous 
fuel to extend a measurement range for heat of gasification. 
The establishment of steady burning of materials in microgravity has not been fully 
established. Anecdotal tests indicate that this is possible. The special nature of burning in a 
purely diffusive environment must be fraught with new effects. Some of these effects have been 
seen among current fundamental research studies on droplets and flame spread over thin 
materials. Other effects involve the small entrainment ambient oxidizer due to the velocity of the 
vaporizing fuel, three- dimensional effects, and the propulsion of flaming droplets and brands 
caused by pressurization during vaporization. Also the effect of radiation feedback, so common 
to fire growth on Earth, has not been fully explored, and is likely to be a factor. 
A serious fire accident occurred on the MIR (Ross, 2001) when a solid propellant oxygen 
generator ignited producing a “blowtorch-like white conical flame” that caused other materials to 
become involved while extinguishment was initiated by the crew. The fire burned out and caused 
extensive smoke damage. Hopefully, a more serious event is not waiting to happen. Yet it is 
likely that the “perfect storm” of conditions can be manifested to produce a serious and sustained 
spacecraft fire accident. The role of materials will be responsible. We should fully understand 
how these materials will behave, and how to relate them to Earth-bound testing. 
 
1.3 Background of combustion in microgravity 
Experiments in Skylab (Ross, 2001; Kimzey, 1974) indicated sustained burning of thin paper and 
plastics. More recent experiments indicate flame spread on thin paper and plastic thin cylinders 
in microgravity (Ross, 2001). Spread on 4.5 mm diameter rods of Delrin, PMMA and HDPE in 
the MIR was achieved in opposed flows down to 1 cm/s. Below that speed, the spread and 
burning ceased (Ross, 2001). Opposed flow spread has been well documented, and appears more 
favorable than concurrent spread. It is indicated that concurrent spread could be limited due to 
upstream vitiation by the transport of combustion products. Opposed flow spread in a quiescent 
atmosphere has been shown to depend on material, thickness, and oxygen concentration (Ross, 
2001). 
Perhaps the most striking example of steady burning has been the burning of candle flames 
on the MIR (Ross, 2001) for periods ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A 
spherical flame formed around the wick. Attempts to repeat this in shuttle flights led to similar, 
but much shorter durations of burning. The MIR flights had atmospheres of 0.22 – 0.25 oxygen

Perhaps the most striking example of steady burning has been the burning of candle flames 
on the MIR (Ross, 2001) for periods ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A 
spherical flame formed around the wick. Attempts to repeat this in shuttle flights led to similar, 
but much shorter durations of burning. The MIR flights had atmospheres of 0.22 – 0.25 oxygen 
mole fraction, with a metal mesh screen surrounding the experiment; while the Shuttle had 0.217 
oxygen fraction and a perforated plastic box enclosing the experiment (Dietrich et al., 2000). 
These differences in containment likely affected the input of fresh air to the candle flame and its 
burning duration. It was noted that the wax melt at the base of the wick distorted into a ball, and 
the flames oscillated before extinction. 
The candle experiments clearly indicate the capability of steady sustained burning in a 
quiescent atmosphere of surface burning. This is also born out in droplet experiments by 
Kumagai and others (Ross, 2001). The droplet flame can be considered quasi-steady as the 
droplet diameter is reduced in burning. The droplet burning rates are slightly less than the ideal 
theoretical thin flame spherical solutions, but the behavior has a similar dependence with droplet 
diameter. Extinction occurs as the drop diameter is decreased, with diffusive effects governing 
small initial drops, and radiative effects for larger droplets. There are other instances of steady

1.5.1 Study of flat surface burning in microgravity 
Initially this study was to consider burning in various gravity space applications, such as the 
Moon and Mars environments. An early consideration was to explore such conditions in aircraft 
gravity simulations. Thus, a test of the burner approach was to consider the burning on a flat 
plate at various inclinations, with burning on top and the bottom. This work allowed us to 
explore this burning configuration by tests with real fuels, with a burner, and through theoretical 
analyses. In short, the results help to establish the credibility and accuracy of the emulation with 
a burner, and the limitations of theory to predict the results. A brief summary of this work 
follows, and Bustamante et al. (2012) presented a recent paper covering it. 
For the inclined plate burning experiments, laminar burning was primarily examined. 
This was done using two liquid fuels, methanol and ethanol, each saturated into a porous ceramic 
wick plate as shown in Figure 3. The plate was oriented at angles of 0º (vertical), and +/_ 30, 60 
and 90º, with negative angles indicating burning on the bottom. Steady burning could be 
achieved for each of these conditions; however, for top burning in particular, at flow distances 
exceeding about 5 cm, the onset of unsteady instabilities occurred. This was not considered fully

Nevertheless, the ability of the burner to emulate the distributive aspects of the burning by 
these flame standoff comparisons is encouraging. It is noteworthy that theoretical analyses to 
achieve similar results are limited by the effects of transition instabilities, variable properties, 
and flame radiation. Even a DNS simulation (Raghavan et al., 2010) of this inclined plate

burning is using a burner, as it automatically accounts for the effects of instabilities, radiation,

1.5.3 Burner design and validation in normal gravity 
A BRE burner prototype has been designed and constructed. Its size has been selected based on 
our flight and drop tower tests, and the burner size used by Brahmi et al. The prototype BRE 
burner was selected to have an operating face of 50 mm in diameter. Due to the anticipated heat 
flux variation over the surface while burning in microgravity or normal gravity, two sensors are 
used. An appropriate averaging of the two heat fluxes should provide the needed average heat 
flux for computing the heat of gasification. The burner is designed with water-cooling to 
maintain reasonable operating temperatures, but thermocouples will directly record the surface 
temperature of the burner allowing the reradiation heat flux to be computed. Brass and glass 
beads provide a porous matrix for metered fuel flow, and porous brass screen serves as its face 
and internal layers. Figure 10 shows photographs of the prototype BRE. It shows the face with a 
heat flux sensor near the center and near the edge. It also shows the fuel and water supply lines 
below. We will perfect the operation of the prototype and establish its accuracy compared to real 
burning of materials. This will provide credibility for the BRE to work for a normal gravity 
environment. In particular, the control of the surface temperature needs to be refined to be able to 
range over a proper range of real fuel temperatures, roughly 50 – 500 ºC. For now we will accept 
the temperatures we get with the prototype 
 We recently tested the BRE prototype to see if it could emulate a 50 mm pool of 
methanol steadily burning. The mass loss rate of methanol was measured and the flame was 
photographed. To match the methanol with the BRE we would need to use a fuel gas with the 
same flow rate. Also to match the flame height and the consequently the heat flux, the fuel must 
have the same heat of combustion. In addition a consideration of the soot tendency was made 
that led to methane as the gaseous fuel. However, nitrogen must be added to the fuel stream so 
that the resulting fuel mixture has a heat of combustion matching that of methanol, 19.1 kJ/g 
(Tewarson). The gas burner BRE used a fuel mixture of 52% (volume) methane with 48% 
nitrogen to achieve the needed heat of combustion. The flow rate of the mixture was 33 cc/s flow 
rate to match the measure steady burning rate of the methanol of 11g/m 2-s.

2. FLIGHT EXPERIMENT 
2.1 Knowledge Lacking and Knowledge to be Gained by Flight Tests 
The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the range of steady burning conditions for 
condensed fuels in microgravity. We will identify the associated material properties and the real 
materials that are represented. Once established based on fuel properties, NASA Test 2 could be 
used as a basis for establishing comparable properties for real materials. This could elevate the 
role of NASA Test 2 over Test 1. This would close the loop of using a ground-based test to 
assess the true flammability of materials in microgravity. 
The BRE mapping of material flammability in microgravity would provide a scientific 
rationale for assessing the fire hazard. We intend to explore the range of heats of combustion 
form about 5 – 50 kJ/g, and heats of gasification from about 0.5 – 5 kJ/g. These properties 
embrace common materials including paper, plastics and liquids. In addition, the BRE concept 
could be exploited in follow-on tests concerned with flowing ambients and extinguishing agents. 
 
2.2 Experimental Objectives 
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity 
ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH 4/N 2 and C2H4/N 2 mixtures 
on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N 2 ambients with various 
pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures Emphasize conditions that can be 
related to diverse condensed fuels. 
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O 2/CO 2 (desired). 
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for ignition limits. 
4. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. 
 
2.3 Summary of Approach 
To accomplish the above objectives, three types of flight experiments are proposed: burning, 
ignition limit, and extinction limit. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to 
verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. 
For each burn test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice 
of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. 
The flames will be observed without varying the fuel or its flow rate. Because burner surface 
temperature and heat flux will vary during the burn, this will allow a broad range of conditions to 
be observed during a single test. 
For each ignition limit test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents. Fuel 
flow will commence followed by attempted ignition.

2.5 Justification for Extended-Duration Microgravity 
As discussed above, NASA Test 1 and Test 2 are currently incapable of directly analyzing 
material fire hazards in spacecraft. While microgravity tests of condensed fuels have been 
performed and are planned, these are not expected to reveal sufficient information about the 
diverse condensed fuels that exist aboard the ISS. The BRE experiment seeks to remedy these 
deficiencies. 
The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft owing to considerable g-
jitter disturbances. While limited testing is possible in drop towers, the characteristic times for 
the gas phase (approximately 20 s) and the burner surface temperature (approximately 40 s) 
preclude consideration of quasi-steady conditions. The long duration testing in the ISS will 
facilitate the efficient operation of the BRE to exploit a relatively quick record of results over a 
range of flow rates. This will insure a complete flammability map in microgravity.

3.5 Post Flight Data Analysis Plan 
The proposed test matrix is intended to shed light on the burning of condensed fuels in 
microgravity. We plan to examine conditions that map out flammable conditions and burning 
rates of diverse condensed fuels. This will result in extensive image data. 
Much of the post-flight data analysis will occur during mission operations as the science 
team evaluates each set of test runs in preparation for subsequent runs. Analysis of these tests 
will include: tracking of flame size and shape; analysis of discrete signals (e.g., thermocouples, 
radiometers, photomultipliers, and pressure transducers) for evidence of the quasi-steadiness of 
the flames; analysis of the temperature profiles (thin filament, soot temperature, and far-field 
thermocouples) to evaluate quasi-steadiness; and de-convolution of soot volume fraction 
measurements. 
The flammability maps will be prepared on 3-axis plots where the axes are burner heat of 
combustion, heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux (See Figure 13). Flame temperatures near 
extinction will be determined either by de-convolution of the soot temperature data or by thin 
fiber pyrometry.
